What was found, and where

Senasica reported one active case in Sonora, in a bovine at Munihuasa, in the municipality of Álamos, about 17 kilometres from the Chihuahua state line. It was announced on 19 August. Nationally, Senasica counted 1,969 active cases in epidemiological week 33, up from 1,818 on 8 August, so a single animal is statistically trivial. Geographically it is not.

Sonora borders Arizona. Until this detection it was one of only three Mexican states with no confirmed screwworm, and it had been officially free of the parasite since 1981, with no case since May 1980. It is now the thirtieth of thirty-two states to record one, leaving only Baja California and Baja California Sur clean. The US Department of Agriculture had identified Sonora, alongside Chihuahua, as a lowest-risk origin for resuming imports — on the strength of its inspection programme and its distance from the southern outbreak rather than simply its case count.

The state response was immediate: a 20-kilometre sanitary cordon around the detection, the release of 360,000 sterile flies, and preventive treatment of animals in the zone with doramectin for adults and a topical product on newborn calves’ umbilical cords. Governor Alfonso Durazo announced the case; the state agriculture secretary, Juan González, set out the technical response.

Why sterile flies

The New World screwworm is a fly whose larvae feed on the living tissue of warm-blooded animals. It was eradicated from North America decades ago using the sterile insect technique: mass-rearing male flies, sterilising them with radiation, and releasing them so that wild females mate without producing offspring.

It works, and it is slow. Each release only suppresses the generation it meets, so the flies have to keep coming until the wild population collapses. Mexico’s flies come from a plant at Metapa de Domínguez in Chiapas, opened by President Sheinbaum in June, which started at 28 million flies a week and is aiming for 100 million a week by the end of the year. The scale needed to hold a barrier across a country the size of Mexico is enormous.

This is why one case in Sonora is treated as an emergency rather than a veterinary footnote. The economic damage comes not from the animal but from what the detection does to the border.

What the border closure has already cost

The suspension of Mexican cattle exports has been expensive. Estimates of the damage range from about US$1.1 billion in income not received by ranchers to roughly US$2.4 billion in lost foreign exchange, depending on which industry figure you take and what period it covers.

The reopening was never going to restore that quickly. CNOG, the national ranchers’ body, expects about 700 head a day at the start, rising to 1,300–1,500 a day, and roughly 40,000 a month through Sonora from September — a fraction of the pre-closure trade, which ran to about 1.26 million head a year worth some US$1.2 billion.

Feedlots and packers on the US side have spent a year sourcing elsewhere. On the Mexican side, ranchers have been carrying animals they cannot sell across a border that has been fully shut for fourteen months and disrupted since November 2024. Roughly 1.7 million head have not crossed.

What the Sonora screwworm case does to the timetable

As of 20 August the staged reopening at Agua Prieta–Douglas was still scheduled for 24 August. Whether it holds is a USDA decision, and the department has moved quickly in both directions before.

The argument for proceeding is that the case is contained, cordoned and being treated, and that a single detection in a state the size of Sonora does not change the risk profile of the specific ranches approved to export. Sonora’s regional cattlemen’s union has publicly urged the USDA to hold the date. The argument against is that a state that has just lost a 45-year clean record is a strange place to restart a trade that was suspended over exactly this parasite.

For anyone with exposure to the cattle trade — ranchers, feedlots, packers, or investors in Mexican or US protein companies — the next few days are the ones that matter. A delay would push the restart past the end of August and into a market that has already repriced beef on the assumption of tight supply.

And for anyone simply living in northern Mexico or the US southwest, the practical point is smaller but real: livestock movement controls, inspections at internal checkpoints, and, if you travel with animals, paperwork that did not exist two years ago.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where was the Sonora screwworm case found? In a bovine at Munihuasa, in the Álamos municipality of southern Sonora, confirmed by Mexico’s animal health authority Senasica and announced on 19 August. It is the state’s first case since May 1980. Does this stop the US cattle border reopening? Not automatically. As of 20 August the staged reopening at Agua Prieta, crossing into Douglas, Arizona, was still set for 24 August. The decision rests with the USDA, which had classed Sonora as a lower-risk state. How much has the closure cost Mexican ranchers? Estimates range from about US$1.1 billion in income not received, on CNOG’s count, to roughly US$2.4 billion in lost foreign exchange on a consultancy estimate — and close to US$3 billion including opportunity cost. Around 1.7 million head have not crossed.

Sources: Senasica — animal health reports; USDA APHIS — New World screwworm; Gobierno del Estado de Sonora

World.title: Prosecutors Raided the Maker of Baly, Brazil’s Cheapest Energy Drink
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts Operation Labirinto Fiscal was launched on Thursday 20 August 2026 by the Gaeco unit of the Santa Catarina public prosecutor’s office.

was launched on Thursday 20 August 2026 by the Gaeco unit of the Santa Catarina public prosecutor’s office. The allegation. Improper generation of ICMS state VAT credits and money laundering, with estimated losses of more than R$500 million (about US$96 million).

Improper generation of ICMS state VAT credits and money laundering, with estimated losses of more than R$500 million (about US$96 million). Thirteen search warrants were served in Tubarão, Santa Catarina, and in Manaus, Amazonas.

were served in Tubarão, Santa Catarina, and in Manaus, Amazonas. The company. Fruts Indústria de Concentrados da Amazônia, which supplies the concentrate behind the Baly brand.

Fruts Indústria de Concentrados da Amazônia, which supplies the concentrate behind the Baly brand. The defence. Fruts says it operates in strict compliance and that its tax benefits were formally granted by the federal revenue service and SUDAM.

Fruts says it operates in strict compliance and that its tax benefits were formally granted by the federal revenue service and SUDAM. No charges yet. This is an investigative phase; nobody has been convicted or formally accused.

If you have bought a can of Baly, you have taken part in one of the most aggressive pricing strategies in Brazilian retail. Prosecutors want to know how it was funded.

The Baly energy drink investigation opened on 20 August is a case about tax credits, but it touches something more familiar: why a can of Baly costs a fraction of what a can of Red Bull costs in the same Brazilian supermarket. Prosecutors in Santa Catarina allege improper ICMS credits worth more than R$500 million (about US$96 million). The company says everything it did was authorised in writing.

A Brazilian supermarket. The case turns on ICMS credits, not on what is in the can. (Photo internet reproduction)

What prosecutors say happened

Operation Labirinto Fiscal — ‘fiscal labyrinth’, for the chain of transactions between group companies in different states — is run by Gaeco, the Santa Catarina public prosecutor’s organised crime task force, supporting the sixth prosecutor’s office in Criciúma, with the Amazonas prosecutor’s office assisting in Manaus. Thirteen search warrants, issued by the state’s specialist organised-crime court, were served on 20 August in Tubarão in Santa Catarina and in Manaus, in Amazonas.

The allegation concerns ICMS, the state-level value added tax that is the single most complicated feature of doing business in Brazil. Because ICMS is charged by states rather than by the federal government, and because states compete for investment by offering ICMS incentives, companies can and do structure production across state lines to accumulate credits.

Prosecutors say a manufacturer bought inputs at inflated prices from a related company in the same group based in Manaus, artificially inflating the ICMS credits generated, and that the investigation also covers money laundering. The R$500 million (about US$96 million) estimate comes from Santa Catarina’s state revenue department.

What the company says

Fruts Indústria de Concentrados da Amazônia, the Manaus supplier at one end of the transactions under investigation, said it received news of the raid with surprise and that it operates in strict compliance with Brazilian tax law.

Its central argument is that the tax benefits it used are provided for in legislation and were formally recognised and granted by competent authorities, including the federal revenue service and SUDAM, the development agency for the Amazon region. The company said it is calm about the regularity of its operations and available to cooperate with investigators.

That defence is not a technicality, but there is a gap in it. The Manaus Free Trade Zone exists precisely to give tax advantages to manufacturers who locate in Amazonas, and thousands of legitimate companies use it — but the benefits Fruts cites were granted by federal bodies, while the money prosecutors say went missing is ICMS, a state tax that Santa Catarina levies. A federal incentive is not a defence to a state assessment. The question a court will have to answer is where a granted incentive ends and an engineered credit begins.

Why the Baly energy drink investigation matters commercially

Baly built its business on price. It arrived in a category dominated by expensive imported brands and sold a similar product at a fraction of the cost, and it now sits in almost every corner shop and petrol station in the country. That kind of price gap has to come from somewhere — cheaper inputs, thinner margins, lower marketing spend, or a lower effective tax burden.

If the tax component turns out to be central, competitors will have a case to make. Brazil’s beverage market is unusually litigious about tax treatment, and a finding against Fruts would invite claims from rivals who paid full freight.

It is also worth noting what this case is not. There is no allegation about the safety or content of the product. Nothing in the operation concerns what is in the can.

The bigger picture for anyone doing business in Brazil

Brazil is midway through the largest overhaul of its consumption taxes in a generation, replacing ICMS and several other levies with a dual VAT over a long transition. One reason that reform was politically possible is exactly the kind of arrangement this operation is examining — the accumulated complexity of state incentives has become something even the states themselves struggle to police.

For foreign companies operating here, the practical lesson is about documentation. Fruts’s defence is that its benefits were granted in writing by named agencies. Whether or not that defence succeeds, it is the only defence available. If your Brazilian operation is claiming a state incentive, the paperwork granting it should be somewhere you can find it in an afternoon.

The case will now move slowly. Search warrants are the beginning of an investigation in Brazil, not the end of one, and it will be months before anyone knows whether charges follow.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Baly energy drink investigation about? Prosecutors in Santa Catarina allege the improper generation of ICMS state VAT credits and money laundering, with estimated losses of more than R$500 million (about US$96 million). Thirteen search warrants were served on 20 August 2026. Has Baly been charged with anything? No. Operation Labirinto Fiscal is an investigative phase. No formal accusation or conviction has been announced, and the company denies wrongdoing. Is the product itself under investigation? No. The case concerns tax credits only. There is no allegation about the safety, labelling or contents of the drink.

Sources: Exame — Baly maker targeted in R$500 million ICMS operation; Ministério Público de Santa Catarina; SUDAM — Amazon development agency

World.title: Two New Polls Just Redrew the Governor Races in Ceará and Pará
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts Ceará is tied. Real Time Big Data puts Elmano de Freitas and Ciro Gomes on 44% each in the first round.

Real Time Big Data puts Elmano de Freitas and Ciro Gomes on 44% each in the first round. And tied in a runoff. A simulated second round gives Elmano 46% to Ciro’s 45% — inside the margin of error.

A simulated second round gives Elmano 46% to Ciro’s 45% — inside the margin of error. The method. 1,600 voters interviewed 15–19 August, margin of error 2 percentage points, 95% confidence, registered with the electoral court as CE-08223/2026.

1,600 voters interviewed 15–19 August, margin of error 2 percentage points, 95% confidence, registered with the electoral court as CE-08223/2026. Pará is not close. AtlasIntel has Hana Ghassan on 48.6% against Dr. Daniel Santos on 40.5% in the first round, from 1,197 interviews.

AtlasIntel has Hana Ghassan on 48.6% against Dr. Daniel Santos on 40.5% in the first round, from 1,197 interviews. Presidential coat-tails. In Ceará, Lula leads Flávio Bolsonaro 66% to 27% in a runoff and 65% to 21% in the first round.

In Ceará, Lula leads Flávio Bolsonaro 66% to 27% in a runoff and 65% to 21% in the first round. Still to come. Fresh Quaest rounds are expected in Pernambuco and Rio de Janeiro; no registration numbers or release dates had been published as of 20 August.

A week ago Datafolha had Ciro Gomes 19 points clear in Ceará. The newest poll has the race level at 44 apiece — which tells you as much about polling as about the candidates.

If you were reading Brazil governor polls a week ago, you would have concluded that Ciro Gomes was running away with Ceará. The poll published on 20 August says the race is exactly level. Nothing dramatic happened in between. This is simply what happens when two different firms, using two different methods, measure the same close contest — and it is worth understanding before October, because Brazil’s state races will shape how the next federal government governs.

Brazil votes on electronic machines. Two new state polls landed on 20 August. (Photo internet reproduction)

Ceará: 44 to 44

Real Time Big Data interviewed 1,600 voters in Ceará between 15 and 19 August and found Elmano de Freitas, the sitting governor, and Ciro Gomes, the former minister and four-time presidential candidate, on 44% each. The margin of error is 2 percentage points at 95% confidence, and the survey is registered with the electoral court as CE-08223/2026.

A simulated runoff between the two produces 46% for Elmano and 45% for Ciro. That is a one-point gap in a poll with a two-point margin — statistically, it is a coin flip.

Compare that with the Datafolha poll published on 13 August, commissioned by O Povo, which had Ciro on 52% to Elmano’s 33% from 1,022 interviews on 10–12 August. Neither firm is wrong. They weight their samples differently and they reach respondents differently, and in a race this tight those choices move the result by far more than the gap between the candidates.

Pará: a clearer picture

Pará is the opposite kind of race. AtlasIntel interviewed 1,197 voters between 14 and 19 August, with a three-point margin of error, registered as PA-04533/2026. It was the first poll published after a leaked private video involving Dr. Daniel Santos. Hana Ghassan of the MDB takes 48.6% in the first round against 40.5% for Dr. Daniel Santos of Podemos. Everyone else is under 1.5%.

A simulated second round barely moves it: Ghassan 49.1%, Santos 41.8%. Blank and spoiled ballots come to 6.4% and 2.7% say they do not know.

Pará matters beyond its own borders. Belém hosted the COP30 climate summit in late 2025, and the state is where Brazil’s arguments about the Amazon, oil at the mouth of the river and federal money for the North all land at once.

What the presidential numbers do to the state races

The same Real Time Big Data fieldwork also tested the presidency — registered separately as BR-08791/2026 — and the numbers there are lopsided. Lula leads Flávio Bolsonaro 66% to 27% in a simulated runoff in the state, and 65% to 21% in the first round.

That is a regional result, not a national one — the Northeast has been Lula’s strongest base for two decades. But it complicates Ciro Gomes’s position. He is running against a governor from Lula’s party in a state where Lula is enormously popular, which means every vote he wins has to be won on local terms rather than national ones.

Reading Brazil governor polls without getting fooled

Three habits will save you from most polling mistakes here. Check the field dates, not the publication date. Check the registration number with the TSE, the electoral court; every legitimate poll has one and the registration names the client — both polls above were commissioned by the firms themselves. And treat any gap smaller than twice the margin of error as no gap at all.

Applied to Ceará, that last rule says the race is tied and has been tied for some time, and that the apparent swing from the earlier Datafolha poll is probably some mixture of method and noise rather than a real collapse in Ciro’s support.

What lands next

Two more states are due. Fresh Quaest rounds are expected in Pernambuco and Rio de Janeiro, but as of 20 August neither registration number nor release date had been published, so treat any circulating numbers with care until they are.

In Pernambuco the last published numbers, from a Genial/Quaest survey fielded 22–26 July with 900 respondents (PE-09649/2026), had Raquel Lyra on 43% and João Campos on 37%. In Rio, a Genial/Quaest poll fielded 21–25 July with 1,200 respondents (RJ-02671/2026) put Eduardo Paes on 38%, with Douglas Ruas and Anthony Garotinho on 10% each. Rio is currently being run on an interim basis by Ricardo Couto, president of the state court of justice, after Cláudio Castro’s resignation.

For foreign residents and investors, state governors are not a footnote. They set state VAT policy, sign infrastructure concessions and control the police. Whoever wins in Recife and Rio will matter to your electricity bill and your commute long after the presidential result stops being news.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is leading the Ceará governor race? Nobody, on the latest numbers. Real Time Big Data’s poll published 20 August has Elmano de Freitas and Ciro Gomes on 44% each, and a simulated runoff at 46% to 45% — both results well inside the two-point margin of error. Why do Brazil governor polls disagree with each other? Different firms use different sampling and weighting methods, and interview at different times. In a race where the candidates are within a point or two of each other, those technical choices move the headline number more than any real shift in opinion does. What are the latest numbers for Pernambuco and Rio de Janeiro? The most recent published figures are from July. Genial/Quaest had Raquel Lyra on 43% to João Campos’s 37% in Pernambuco, and Eduardo Paes on 38% in Rio. Newer rounds are expected but had not been registered or released as of 20 August.

Sources: Poder360 — AtlasIntel Pará; Valor — Quaest Pernambuco registration; Tribunal Superior Eleitoral — poll registry

World.title: Colombia’s Own Economists Have Given Up on Cheaper Money This Year
World.content:
Colombia · Economy

Key Facts 6.6% for end-2026. That is the median analyst forecast for total inflation in the central bank’s monthly expectations survey.

That is the median analyst forecast for total inflation in the central bank’s monthly expectations survey. Revised upward. The same survey read 6.3% in April, so forecasters have added three-tenths of a point.

The same survey read 6.3% in April, so forecasters have added three-tenths of a point. Rate on hold. Fedesarrollo’s August financial opinion survey has analysts expecting the policy rate to stay at 12% in September and again in December.

Fedesarrollo’s August financial opinion survey has analysts expecting the policy rate to stay at 12% in September and again in December. A softer expectation than last month. In July the same panel had been pencilling in 12.50% for December, so the direction of travel is toward no change rather than a hike.

In July the same panel had been pencilling in 12.50% for December, so the direction of travel is toward no change rather than a hike. Next decision: 30 September 2026. That is the next scheduled meeting of the central bank’s board.

That is the next scheduled meeting of the central bank’s board. Where the peso sits. The official TRM was 3,053 on 20 August and the dollar closed the interbank session near 3,062 — the peso’s strongest level in more than seven years.

Two separate surveys point the same way: prices are proving stickier than hoped, and the 12% policy rate is not coming down before Christmas.

If you earn in Colombian pesos, or you are paid abroad and spend in Bogotá, Colombia inflation expectations are the number that quietly sets your year. The latest reading is not what anyone wanted. Analysts polled by the Banco de la República now put total inflation at 6.6% by the end of 2026 — up from 6.3% in April — and a separate survey of the same community says the 12% policy rate is going nowhere before December.

Banco de la Republica in Bogota. Its analyst survey now sees 6.6% inflation at end-2026. (Photo internet reproduction)

What the central bank’s survey actually says

The Banco de la República runs a monthly survey of economic analysts. The round that produced the 6.6% figure was fielded between 8 and 10 July and the number surfaced in the bank’s own commentary in mid-August. It is a median, meaning half the forecasters are above it and half below.

Three-tenths of a percentage point does not sound like much. In practice it is the difference between a story where inflation is converging on target and a story where it has settled into a plateau. Colombia’s target is 3%, with a tolerance band of one point either side. At 6.6%, the country would end 2026 at more than double the top of that band.

Why the interest rate is stuck at 12%

Here it is worth separating two surveys that are often blurred together. The 6.6% inflation figure comes from the central bank’s own analyst poll. The interest-rate expectation comes from Fedesarrollo’s Encuesta de Opinión Financiera, a different survey run by a Bogotá think tank.

The next rate decision falls on 30 September 2026, and Fedesarrollo’s August round says analysts expect the board to leave the rate at 12% then, and to still have it at 12% in December. Fedesarrollo’s own inflation median for end-2026, 6.53%, sits within a rounding error of the central bank survey’s 6.6%. That is actually a dovish revision: in July the same panel had expected 12.50% by year-end, which would have meant a hike.

So the market has stopped fearing higher rates. It has not started expecting lower ones.

What it costs you

A 12% policy rate feeds through to mortgage and consumer credit pricing with a lag of months. If you are shopping for a property loan in Colombia, the arithmetic in 2026 is unforgiving and it is unlikely to improve before the first quarter of 2027 at the earliest.

On the other side of the ledger, savers are being paid properly for the first time in years. Fixed-term deposits and government paper are yielding real returns even against 6.6% inflation, which is not something you could say in 2021.

And if you are converting foreign income, the peso has been firming through the month — the TRM was 3,053 on 20 August against 3,128.65 two days earlier, its strongest in more than seven years, though the dollar ticked up on the day itself. A stronger peso is good news for Colombians buying imported goods and bad news for anyone whose salary arrives in dollars.

The political layer nobody can price

President Abelardo de la Espriella took office on 7 August and has promised a tax reform, without yet publishing the bill. The central bank is independent, but its board reads fiscal policy closely, and a reform that widens the deficit would make rate cuts harder to justify.

There is also the earthquake. The 10 August quake, magnitude 7.4, killed at least 289 people and hit Chocó hardest; Colombia declared an economic emergency and has put the preliminary damage bill at US$9.57 billion. Reconstruction spending is necessary and it is also inflationary, particularly in construction materials and labour. None of that is captured in a July survey.

How to read Colombia inflation expectations from here

Two dates are worth putting in a calendar. DANE, the statistics agency, publishes the next monthly inflation print in the first week of September, and the board meets on 30 September. If inflation surprises downward and the peso holds its recent strength, the December expectation will start to move.

Until then, plan on borrowing being expensive and cash being reasonably well paid. That is an unusual combination, and it favours anyone sitting on savings over anyone trying to build with borrowed money.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are Colombia inflation expectations for the end of 2026? The median analyst forecast in the Banco de la República’s monthly expectations survey is 6.6% for total inflation at end-2026, up from 6.3% in the April round. Will Colombia’s central bank cut interest rates in 2026? Analysts surveyed by Fedesarrollo in August do not think so. They expect the policy rate to stay at 12% at the 30 September meeting and to still be at 12% in December — a softer view than July, when the same panel expected 12.50%. Is this the same survey as Fedesarrollo’s? No. The 6.6% inflation figure comes from the central bank’s own analyst survey, fielded 8–10 July. The interest-rate expectation comes from Fedesarrollo’s separate Encuesta de Opinión Financiera for August. They are often quoted together, which causes confusion.

Sources: Banco de la República — analyst expectations survey; Portafolio — Fedesarrollo financial opinion survey; RT — USD/COP daily close

World.title: Chile’s Main Stock Index Changes Hands, and Gains a Member on 1 September
World.content:
Chile · Business

Key Facts From 1 September 2026 the index is administered by MSCI, replacing S&P Dow Jones Indices, and becomes the MSCI IPSA.

the index is administered by MSCI, replacing S&P Dow Jones Indices, and becomes the MSCI IPSA. Pampa Investments returns , taking the constituent count to 31. It was in the index as Oro Blanco until about two years ago.

, taking the constituent count to 31. It was in the index as Oro Blanco until about two years ago. No fixed size. The number of members will now vary according to size and liquidity rather than being capped at 30.

The number of members will now vary according to size and liquidity rather than being capped at 30. Free-float weighting. Selection and weighting use market capitalisation adjusted for the shares actually available to trade.

Selection and weighting use market capitalisation adjusted for the shares actually available to trade. Reviewed four times a year instead of on the previous schedule.

instead of on the previous schedule. Who Pampa is. Formerly Oro Blanco, it is the vehicle through which the Ponce Lerou family holds its 25% stake in lithium producer SQM. Francisca Ponce puts its market value at around US$3.8 billion, with a 29% free float.

Since 2018 the IPSA has held 30 companies on S&P methodology. From next month it holds however many qualify, on MSCI’s — starting with 31.

The Chile IPSA index has looked broadly the same since 2018: 30 companies, rebalanced twice a year, run to S&P Dow Jones methodology. From 1 September 2026 that changes. MSCI takes over, the fixed 30-stock ceiling disappears, and the first consequence is that Pampa Investments returns to the index, bringing the count to 31.

The Santiago exchange. MSCI takes over the IPSA methodology on 1 September. (Photo internet reproduction)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

What actually changes

Three things. First, the index will no longer have a fixed number of constituents — membership is determined by size and liquidity thresholds, so the count can drift up or down. Second, selection and weighting move to free-float adjusted market capitalisation, meaning a company’s weight reflects the shares genuinely available to buy rather than its total shares outstanding. Third, the index is reviewed four times a year.

Free-float adjustment matters more in Chile than in most markets. Chilean listed companies are unusually concentrated, with controlling families and pension funds holding large blocks that never trade. Weighting by total capitalisation overstates how investable those companies are; weighting by free float corrects it.

The published coverage of this first rebalance names Pampa’s return and the move to 31 constituents. It does not identify a company being removed, which is consistent with a methodology that no longer requires one out for one in. The handover is part of nuam, the merger bringing the Chilean, Colombian and Peruvian exchanges onto a common footing, and the broader IGPA expands to 50 members at the same time.

Who Pampa Investments is

Pampa Investments is the renamed Oro Blanco, reorganised as part of a simplification of the Pampa group’s corporate structure. Through it, the group associated with Julio Ponce Lerou holds its interest in SQM, the lithium and speciality chemicals producer that is one of Chile’s most internationally significant companies.

It is now led by Francisca Ponce, his daughter and vice-president of Grupo Pampa, who puts the company’s market value at around US$3.8 billion with a free float of 29%. She has been preparing an international roadshow aimed at bringing foreign investors onto the register. The restructuring has already worked on one measure: the holding discount narrowed from a ten-year average of about 50% to under 20%.

Index inclusion is exactly what that campaign needs. Funds that track or benchmark against the IPSA have to hold what the index holds, so entry generates buying that has nothing to do with anyone’s view of the company.

Why the Chile IPSA index change matters to investors

If you hold a Chilean equity fund, or an emerging-markets fund with Chilean exposure, your portfolio is about to shift without you doing anything. Free-float weighting will reduce the index weight of tightly held companies and increase it for those with wider public ownership.

For the market as a whole, handing the index to MSCI is a credibility move. MSCI methodology is what global allocators already understand, and an index built to a familiar standard is easier to benchmark against, easier to build products on and easier to explain to a committee in London.

The index itself has been strong, trading around 11,240 to 11,250 through the week of the announcement, while the peso closed near 925 to the US dollar on 20 August. Chile has been one of the better-performing markets in the region this year, helped by copper and by a government that markets read as investment-friendly. Pampa’s own shares led the Santiago market on 20 August, up 1.4% on the inclusion news, with the stock still outside the index.

The catch

Quarterly reviews cut both ways. More frequent rebalancing keeps the index current, but it also means more forced trading, and in a market as thin as Chile’s, forced trading has a cost. A stock entering or leaving the IPSA moves further on the announcement than it would in a deeper market.

There is also a concentration question that the new methodology does not solve. The Chilean market is dominated by a handful of large groups, and adding a holding company whose principal asset is a 25% stake in another listed company arguably increases the double-counting rather than reducing it. Investors buying the index now own a slice of SQM directly and another slice of it through Pampa.

None of that is a reason to avoid the market. It is a reason to look at what you own rather than assuming the index does the diversifying for you.

The first rebalance takes effect on 1 September. The next review under the new schedule will be the first real test of how much the changed methodology moves things.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is changing about the Chile IPSA index? From 1 September 2026 MSCI takes over administration from S&P Dow Jones Indices. The fixed 30-company limit disappears, weighting moves to free-float adjusted market capitalisation, and the index is reviewed four times a year instead of twice. Which company is joining the IPSA? Pampa Investments, formerly Oro Blanco, returns from 1 September, taking the index to 31 constituents. Francisca Ponce puts its market value at around US$3.8 billion, with a free float of 29%. Is any company being removed? The coverage of this first rebalance does not name an exclusion. Under the new methodology the index no longer has a fixed number of members, so an addition does not require a removal.

Sources: Diario Financiero — Pampa Investments enters the IPSA; La Tercera Pulso — Francisca Ponce roadshow; RT — IPSA and USD/CLP daily close

World.title: Colombia Israel Visa Waiver Returns From 1 September, 14 Months After It Was Scrapped
World.content:
Colombia · Politics

Key Facts Effective 1 September 2026, as announced by Israel’s foreign ministry. Colombia’s Cancillería had not published its own statement or decree as of 20 August.

as announced by Israel’s foreign ministry. Colombia’s Cancillería had not published its own statement or decree as of 20 August. It works both ways. Israelis travelling to Colombia and Colombians travelling to Israel are both covered.

Israelis travelling to Colombia and Colombians travelling to Israel are both covered. Agreed by the foreign ministers. Israel’s Gideon Sa’ar and Colombia’s Omar Bula Escobar negotiated the arrangement.

Israel’s Gideon Sa’ar and Colombia’s Omar Bula Escobar negotiated the arrangement. A restoration, not a novelty. The two countries dropped their reciprocal exemption only in July 2025; before that, citizens of each travelled to the other without a visa.

The two countries dropped their reciprocal exemption only in July 2025; before that, citizens of each travelled to the other without a visa. Part of a wider thaw. President Abelardo de la Espriella, in office since 7 August, has restored ties with Israel; on 14 August he separately dismissed five Petro-appointed ambassadors who had refused to resign.

President Abelardo de la Espriella, in office since 7 August, has restored ties with Israel; on 14 August he separately dismissed five Petro-appointed ambassadors who had refused to resign. Not yet in force. The announcement came on 20 August; the waiver does not apply to travel before 1 September.

The visa requirement is only fourteen months old. From next month it disappears again, and the two countries are back where they were before the rupture.

The Colombia Israel visa waiver announced on 20 August is the clearest sign yet of how fast Colombia’s foreign policy has turned. From 1 September 2026, Colombians can fly to Tel Aviv and Israelis can fly to Bogotá without applying for a visa first. What makes it striking is how recent the requirement is: the two countries only scrapped their mutual exemption in July 2025.

Tel Aviv. Colombians could travel here without a visa until July 2025, and will again from 1 September. (Photo internet reproduction)

What changes, and when

The arrangement is a mutual exemption from the visa requirement, agreed between foreign ministers Gideon Sa’ar and Omar Bula Escobar and announced by Israel’s foreign ministry. It takes effect on 1 September 2026. Colombia’s Cancillería had published no statement or decree of its own by the end of 20 August.

The stated purpose is ordinary enough: tourism, business travel and commercial exchange. Colombia has been trying to widen its tourism base beyond North America and Europe for years, and Israel sends a large number of long-stay travellers to South America, particularly young people travelling after military service. Until July 2025, when the two countries dropped their reciprocal exemption, Colombia was one of the easier stops on that circuit.

One practical caution. The announcement was made on 20 August. If you are travelling before 1 September, the old requirements still apply. Check with the consulate rather than assuming.

How Colombia got here in two years

In May 2024, President Gustavo Petro severed diplomatic relations with Israel over the war in Gaza, which he described as a genocide. Colombia had been one of Israel’s closest defence partners in Latin America, and the break was not symbolic — it touched arms procurement, intelligence sharing and coal exports.

Petro’s term ended on 7 August 2026. His successor, Abelardo de la Espriella, campaigned on restoring the relationship and re-established ties immediately; on 14 August he separately dismissed five ambassadors appointed by Petro who had declined to submit protocol resignations. A decree to end the ban on coal exports to Israel is ready.

The visa waiver is the piece of that reversal most likely to affect ordinary people rather than governments.

What it means if you live in Colombia

If you hold Colombian citizenship, you get back a destination you could reach paperwork-free until July 2025. If you hold Israeli citizenship and are among the foreign residents in Medellín, Bogotá or Santa Marta, your family can visit without a consular appointment again.

For businesses, the effect is smaller but real. Israel is a significant buyer of Colombian coal and coffee and a significant seller of agricultural technology, water systems and security equipment. Removing the visa step does not create trade on its own, but it removes friction from the visits that precede trade.

There is also a tourism angle worth watching. Colombia’s Caribbean coast and coffee region already draw a steady Israeli backpacker flow that currently routes through Peru and Bolivia. Making entry simpler will move some of that volume.

The Colombia Israel visa waiver still has open questions

Several details have not been published. No Colombian decree number has appeared, and neither government has said how long visa-free stays will last. The arrangement that ran until July 2025 gives the benchmark: Colombians entered Israel for up to 90 days, and Israelis could spend up to 180 cumulative days in Colombia in any 365.

Nor is it clear whether the waiver covers all passport types or only ordinary passports. Diplomatic and service passports are usually handled separately.

And the wider relationship is still moving. Colombia has announced it will relocate its embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem — a step far more contentious at home and abroad than a visa arrangement — and has recognised Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights. Sa’ar has described the direction of travel as a return to a strategic alliance.

For now, though, the practical takeaway is simple. From 1 September, one fewer form.

How this fits Colombia’s wider reopening

The visa move is not happening in isolation. Since taking office, the De la Espriella government has replaced ambassadors, floated a tax reform it has yet to publish, and had to declare an economic emergency after the 10 August earthquake, whose preliminary damage bill Colombia puts at US$9.57 billion.

In that context, a visa waiver is cheap diplomacy. It costs the treasury nothing, it delivers a visible result within weeks, and it signals to Washington and Jerusalem that Colombia’s foreign policy has changed direction without requiring a single peso of new spending.

Whether it lasts is a different question. Colombia’s relationship with Israel swung hard in one direction under Petro and has swung hard back within a month of the new government taking office. Anyone planning travel or business on the strength of it should keep that volatility in mind: this exemption has now been scrapped once and reinstated once inside fourteen months, and nothing about the arrangement makes it harder to reverse a third time.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does the Colombia Israel visa waiver start? On 1 September 2026. The agreement was announced on 20 August 2026 and does not apply to travel before that date. Does the waiver apply to both countries’ citizens? Yes. It is a mutual exemption, covering Israelis travelling to Colombia and Colombians travelling to Israel. Why did Colombians need a visa for Israel in the first place? They did not, until July 2025. Gustavo Petro severed diplomatic ties in May 2024 over the war in Gaza and the mutual visa exemption was dropped the following year. Abelardo de la Espriella restored relations after taking office on 7 August 2026.

Sources: La República — Colombia and Israel drop visa requirement; Semana — visa requirement eliminated; Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs

World.title: Costa Rica President Sends Eight Major Proposals to Congress
World.content:
President Laura Fernández has presented eight new bills that could change how Costa Rica handles pensions, loans, government contracts, internet funding and several other public programs. The proposals were announced as Fernández marked her first 100 days in office. However, none of the changes has taken effect. Each bill must first be discussed and approved by the Legislative Assembly.

Here is what the eight bills would do in simple terms:

Provide more pensions for people in need

The first bill would move part of an employer-paid payroll contribution into the fund that provides basic pensions to older adults and people with disabilities who did not pay enough into the regular pension system. The government estimates that the change could provide pensions to around 31,000 additional people.

The proposal would not take money from workers’ individual retirement accounts. Instead, it would redirect money currently sent to Banco Popular.

Limit some powers of the Comptroller General

Another bill would reduce the Comptroller General’s ability to stop or interfere with certain government projects and contracts. The Comptroller is responsible for checking how public money is spent. Under the proposal, its work would focus more narrowly on whether public funds are being handled legally.

Supporters may argue that this would help government projects move faster. Critics are likely to say it could weaken an important check on public spending. Similar ideas appeared in earlier “Jaguar” proposals, parts of which faced constitutional objections. This bill is therefore expected to receive close legal and political attention.

Allow faster government purchasing in special cases

The government also wants public institutions to have a quicker way to purchase goods or services when there is an urgent risk or when the usual bidding process does not fit the situation. An institution would have to explain why the normal process is unsuitable, how it selected the supplier, how much it will spend and how long the contract will last.

The Comptroller would then have 15 working days to review the request. A lack of response would not automatically mean approval.

Give INA more control over hiring

One proposal would create a separate employment system for the National Learning Institute, known as INA. Existing employees could remain under the current Civil Service system. New employees would enter the new system, while current workers could choose to transfer without losing the rights they have already earned.

INA’s board would also receive more freedom to create, remove and classify jobs. The government says this would help the institution respond more quickly to Costa Rica’s training and employment needs.

Move forward with Ciudad Gobierno

Another bill would create special rules for Ciudad Gobierno, a planned group of office buildings intended to bring dozens of government departments together in one location. The Finance Ministry could lease the buildings for up to 30 years, with the possibility of extending the agreement to a maximum of 50 years. The Central American Bank for Economic Integration, known as BCIE, would play a central role in developing the project.

The government says Ciudad Gobierno could save approximately $26 million a year by reducing the amount it pays to rent offices around San José. The proposal includes the possible relocation of as many as 35 public institutions and departments. Parts of the plan involving public land and property used by the Liceo de Costa Rica could become controversial.

Help farmers and fishers buy insurance

The sixth bill would create an agricultural insurance fund called Fonagro. The fund would help farmers, livestock producers, fishers and aquaculture businesses pay for insurance against losses caused by weather, disease and other emergencies.

Small producers and artisanal fishers could receive assistance covering up to 75% of their insurance premiums. Medium-sized producers could receive help covering up to 50%. Money for the program could come from the National Insurance Institute, the Agriculture Ministry and the Rural Development Institute, depending on available funds.

Change who manages money for internet access

The government wants to move responsibility for the National Telecommunications Fund, known as Fonatel, from the telecommunications regulator Sutel to Costa Rica’s Innovation and Research Promoter. Fonatel uses money collected from telecommunications companies to improve internet and telephone access in communities where private companies may not provide adequate service.

The Science, Innovation, Technology and Telecommunications Ministry would also receive greater control over the annual fee paid by telecommunications companies. Existing Fonatel contracts and projects would remain valid during an 18-month transition.

Change how maximum interest rates are calculated

The final bill would change the system Costa Rica uses to set maximum legal interest rates. Costa Rica currently has a formula intended to prevent lenders from charging extremely high interest. Under the proposal, the financial regulator Sugef would calculate new limits each year using a method approved by Conassif, the country’s financial oversight council.

Different types of loans could have different limits. For example, credit cards, personal loans and small-business loans might no longer share the same maximum rate. The proposal would not immediately remove interest-rate limits. However, the new calculation method could result in some limits rising or falling. The final effect on borrowers would depend on the formula adopted by regulators.

What happens next?

The eight bills will now have to move through the Legislative Assembly. Lawmakers can approve, reject or change them during the process. Some proposals, particularly the plan to limit the Comptroller’s powers, may also face questions about whether they comply with Costa Rica’s Constitution.

For now, pensions, interest-rate limits, government purchasing rules and other programs remain unchanged.

World.title: Argentine Thiago Tirante Extends Dream Cincinnati Run Into Quarterfinals
World.content:
Thiago Agustín Tirante’s breakthrough week at the Cincinnati Open continued Wednesday as the Argentine rallied past Jakub Mensik to reach the first ATP Masters 1000 quarterfinal of his career. Tirante recovered after losing a tight opening set to defeat the 14th-seeded Czech 5-7, 6-4, 6-4. The victory sets up a Thursday night quarterfinal against France’s Arthur Fils, who eliminated fifth-seeded Alex de Minaur 6-3, 6-4.

Their match is scheduled for no earlier than 8:30 p.m. on P&G Stadium Court. The 25-year-old Tirante arrived in Cincinnati at a career-high No. 50 in the ATP rankings. He will leave with another significant jump after putting together the best Masters 1000 tournament of his career.

His run began with a routine first-round victory over Jan Choinski, but the tournament changed when he faced Novak Djokovic in the second round. Djokovic dominated the opening set before Tirante turned the match around, defeating the 24-time Grand Slam champion 2-6, 6-4, 6-4. It was the biggest victory of the Argentine’s career and immediately placed him among the tournament’s biggest stories.

Tirante then showed that the Djokovic result was more than a one-match surprise. He defeated Spain’s Martin Landaluce 7-6(5), 7-6(4) before producing another comeback against Mensik, the No. 16 player in the world. After Mensik edged the first set Wednesday, Tirante stayed aggressive from the baseline and found the breaks he needed in each of the final two sets. He closed the match after two hours and 15 minutes, becoming the last Latin American player remaining in the men’s singles draw.

The result also puts Tirante in select company. He joins Francisco Cerúndolo as one of only two active Argentine men to have reached an ATP Masters 1000 quarterfinal. Tirante’s rise has developed gradually. He finished 2019 as the world’s top-ranked junior and won the Roland Garros boys’ doubles title that year. His progress on the professional circuit took longer, with much of his early success coming at Challenger tournaments.

He broke into the ATP Top 100 in 2024 and has made another move this season. Before arriving in Cincinnati, Tirante reached the third round in Madrid and the fourth round in both Rome and Montreal. He also advanced to the semifinals of the ATP tournament in Houston, where he defeated Ben Shelton.

His next challenge will be Fils, the 21st seed and one of the most consistent Masters 1000 performers of the season. The 22-year-old Frenchman has reached the quarterfinals or better at five Masters events in 2026. Tirante, however, has already beaten two seeded players and one of the greatest players in tennis history this week. One more victory would send an Argentine man into the Cincinnati semifinals and extend a run that has become one of the tournament’s most unexpected stories.

World.title: New Digital Platform to provide data on 194 Belizean communities
World.content:
New Digital Platform to provide data on 194 Belizean communities

By Zoila Palma: The International Organization for Migration (IOM), in partnership with the Ministry of Rural Transformation, has launched the Community Profile Information System (CPIS), a new digital platform designed to collect, store and analyze critical information from 194 communities across Belize.

The platform was developed from an IOM-led pilot survey conducted in 2023, which gathered socioeconomic and demographic data from 20 rural communities in southern Belize.

Building on that initiative, CPIS is being funded by the IOM through the Government of the United States to make reliable community information more accessible to decision-makers, development partners and local stakeholders.

The system is expected to strengthen evidence-based planning and improve service delivery by providing timely information on community needs, resources and opportunities. It will also enhance access to community and business data, supporting more targeted and inclusive development programs across the country.

The IOM said CPIS will give stakeholders a stronger information base for identifying priorities and designing interventions that respond to the realities of Belizean communities.

The platform is available online at communityprofile.ruraltransformation.gov.bz.

World.title: Man busted with three bullets has until Friday to decide if he will accept 1-year-4-month sentence or plead not guilty and face trial; Complains he is being kept ‘in the hole’ in jail and doesn’t like it
World.content:
Man busted with three bullets has until Friday to decide if he will accept 1-year-4-month sentence or plead not guilty and face trial; Complains he is being kept ‘in the hole’ in jail and doesn’t like it

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Justin Stephen Goff, 38, who was charged earlier this year after police allegedly found him with three live rounds of ammunition, is considering changing his not guilty plea after receiving a sentencing indication from the Magistrate’s Court.

Goff appeared unrepresented before a Magistrate in Court #3, where he sought an indication of the sentence he could receive if he pleaded guilty to keeping ammunition without a gun licence.

The Magistrate informed Goff that a fine would not be considered and that he would instead face a custodial sentence. After taking into account aggravating and mitigating factors, as well as a one-third reduction for an early guilty plea, the court indicated that Goff could receive a sentence of approximately one year and four months in prison.

Goff was given until Friday, August 21, to decide whether to accept the sentencing indication and change his plea or proceed to trial.

During the hearing, Goff complained about his current prison conditions, telling the court that, as a repeat offender, he has been kept in “the hole” since returning to prison in April.

“That’s not a place I like to be,” Goff told the court.

Goff was first arraigned on April 7, 2026, and pleaded not guilty to keeping unlicensed ammunition. Police allege that on April 3 he was found with three live rounds — two S&B-brand rounds and one Aguila-brand round.

At his arraignment, Goff denied the allegation and claimed that the ammunition had been planted on him by the same police officer who later arrested and charged him.

Goff is expected back in court on Friday, when he must indicate whether he will accept the proposed sentence and plead guilty or continue with his case to trial.

World.title: Government of Belize secures landmark agreement to protect Turneffe Atoll
World.content:
Government of Belize secures landmark agreement to protect Turneffe Atoll

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize has secured a landmark agreement aimed at strengthening the long-term protection of Turneffe Atoll and its natural resources.

The Turneffe Conservation Land Trust Deed of Mutual Release, Compromise, and Settlement was signed on August 19, 2026, transforming an earlier agreement between the Government and the Turneffe Atoll Trust into a broader national conservation arrangement.

Under the new agreement, approximately 17,000 acres will remain national lands under public ownership. The Government will hold the lands in an irrevocable conservation trust for the benefit of the people of Belize, ensuring that the area remains protected for present and future generations.

The agreement also establishes an important role for the Turneffe Atoll Sustainability Association (TASA) in managing the lands, while maintaining the participation of the Turneffe Atoll Trust.

It further strengthens protection for three critical flats-fishing habitats within the Turneffe Atoll Marine Reserve, which support Belize’s multi-million-dollar flats-fishing industry and species including bonefish, permit and tarpon.

Prime Minister John Briceño described the agreement as a significant step for Belize’s conservation and development goals. “These lands remain Belizean lands. They remain under public ownership. And they are being secured permanently for present and future generations of Belizeans,” Briceño said. He added that the agreement could usher in “an even stronger era of conservation, science, sustainable livelihoods, and responsible development at Turneffe Atoll.”

The agreement also secures BZ$2.2 million toward the establishment of a marine research facility at Turneffe Atoll through the University of Belize.

The Turneffe Atoll Trust has committed to helping the university mobilize up to approximately BZ$5 million in additional funding for marine research, supporting areas such as fisheries and ecosystem studies, climate and blue-carbon science, field training, international research partnerships and innovation within Belize’s blue economy.

The Prime Minister also acknowledged the Turneffe Atoll Trust, Senator Christopher Coye and the government team involved in the negotiations, along with the Ministry of Natural Resources, Petroleum and Mining, Ministry of Blue Economy and Marine Conservation, Coastal Zone Management Authority and Institute, Attorney General’s Ministry, University of Belize and other technical and legal partners.

World.title: Every vote counts! Help Faith Edgar fly the Belizean flag at Miss World
World.content:
Every vote counts! Help Faith Edgar fly the Belizean flag at Miss World

Belize is being called on to rally behind Miss World Belize, Faith Edgar, as public voting continues for the 73rd Miss World competition in Vietnam.

Faith is currently representing Belize among delegates from around the world and is competing within the Americas and Caribbean region. Supporters in Belize and abroad can now cast their votes through the official Miss World voting platform to help strengthen her position in the competition.
