World.title: Three varieties of 'vegan Dracula' lampreys found in unlikely places
World.content:
With its suction-cup mouth and circular rows of sharp teeth, a close-up view of an Australian brook lamprey is rather frightening.

But unlike many bloodthirsty lampreys around the world, this species prefers a plant-based diet, gobbling up organic matter on creek beds instead.

Scientists only confirmed the discovery of the Australian brook lamprey in 2024. (Supplied: David Moffatt)

The jawless fish measures just 10 centimetres in length, making it difficult to spot in the wild.

Griffith University aquatic ecologist Luke Carpenter-Bundhoo has become somewhat of a lamprey whisperer.

Luke Carpenter-Bundhoo looks for lampreys in a freshwater stream on K'gari. (Supplied: Griffith University)

He unearthed the species by accident on K'gari in 2022 while studying the impacts of the Black Summer bushfires on the island's ecosystem.

"There's about 50 lamprey species throughout the planet and most of them are parasitic, they suck onto the side of a fish and either eat some flesh or drink some blood," Dr Carpenter-Bundhoo said.

" These guys are non-parasitic so they're kind of like a vegan Dracula. "

The discovery led him to team up with Queensland's Department of Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation (DETSI) principal scientist David Moffatt.

The pair has since found two more slightly smaller, as yet unnamed varieties of non-parasitic lampreys.

Loading...

Mr Moffatt first stumbled across the Queensland species in the Noosa River catchment in 2004, but initially believed the fish were "just vagrants" from southern states.

"We kept finding these things just on and off for eight years, and it was fairly obvious then that there was a resident population. They looked quite different as well," Mr Moffatt said.

David Moffatt and Luke Carpenter-Bundhoo have been examining the lampreys at Griffith University's Nathan campus. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

The scientists have since found the tropical lampreys in the most unlikely of places, including on the Sunshine Coast below the Bruce Highway, and as far north as Rockhampton.

"They're existing in these really fragmented populations so they're quite at risk because these are a freshwater fish," Dr Carpenter-Bundhoo said.

"They can't swim out to the ocean and then just pop back into the next creek. They can't go across the land because they're aquatic.

" If something happens to one of those populations it's kind of a big deal. "

The researchers were surprised to discover the fish in Coochin Creek on Queensland's Sunshine Coast. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Ancient secrets unlocked

There are five species of lamprey in the Southern Hemisphere, and Australian brook lamprey (Mordacia praecox) is listed as endangered.

The scientists have just received a $90,000 Queensland government research grant to expand their research.

"These animals aren't necessarily in remote locations; they're just very cryptic, and they're very hard to see," Mr Moffatt said.

" We're at the risk of silent extinction, where we have things go extinct that we didn't even know were existing. "

Luke Carpenter-Bundhoo has been studying the lampreys, which begin the first few years of life in larval form. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

Dr Carpenter-Bundhoo said knowing their locations would increase opportunities for their protection, although lampreys have been around for a long time.

They are known as living fossils.

"They are older than, say, the Australian lungfish, which everybody likes to tout as the dinosaur fish," Dr Carpenter-Bundhoo said.

"Lampreys actually existed before and after dinosaurs. What we see 150 million years ago is effectively what we see as a lamprey today."

A group of Australian brook lampreys was uncovered on K'gari. (Supplied: Griffith University)

He said they were used as a "model organism" for genetic research.

"This is an essential blueprint on how to make a vertebrate," Dr Carpenter-Bundoo said.

" So anything we find with them we may be able to apply to more sophisticated organisms, like humans. "

World.title: Rise in Kimberley animal abuse cases linked to cost of living
World.content:
Mounting financial pressures are leading to an increase in animal cruelty reports, according to the RSPCA, with the problem especially acute in Western Australia's far north.

WARNING: This story contains images of an emaciated animal and animal neglect readers may find distressing.

The organisation said cases of animal abuse in the Kimberley had risen 23 per cent in the past financial year, and it had doubled its intake of animals from the region.

RSPCA WA spokesperson Louise Rowe said in many cases, the neglect appeared to stem from cost-of-living strains.

There has been a rise in the number of malnourished, neglected animals in the Kimberley. (Supplied: RSPCA )

"We're seeing really emaciated animals because they're not being fed enough. We're seeing animals with chronic skin conditions because they're not getting parasite treatments," she said.

" We're seeing animals suffering from ailments that really could have been fixed a lot sooner if they received proper medical care. "

The increase has prompted the charity to provide community outreach days in Broome and Derby, offering free pet health checks, microchipping, pet food and flea and worm treatments.

'No excuse'

There are "undoubtedly" more cases of abuse happening across the Kimberley that the charity does not know about, Ms Rowe said.

She said RSPCA relied on the community to be its "eyes and ears" and urged people who had animal welfare concerns to reach out.

"We know people are struggling. We know that times are tough, but that's no excuse to let your animals suffer," Ms Rowe said.

"Animals should be cared for. They can't do it for themselves, and owners have a responsibility to reach out sooner rather than later."

The RSPCA urged the community to report instances of animal abuse. (Supplied: RSPCA )

RSPCA WA appointed an inspector in the Kimberley in 2022 after the region recorded some of the highest animal cruelty in the state.

But the role was scrapped when it became apparent the lone inspector's safety was at risk.

"We've introduced a fly-in, fly-out model, which is working really well," Ms Rowe said.

"If we get a report that needs urgent action, we can attend ourselves, or we work with others in the area as well that can help us on the ground."

Charities overrun

Saving Animals From Euthanasia (SAFE) Broome is the only animal rescue organisation in town.

Coordinator Sonya Debenham said the biggest challenge was finding foster homes.

Sonya Debenham says vet bills for the animals can cost between $10,000 and $15,000 a month. (Supplied: SAFE)

This challenge has only been compounded by the noticeable increase of cats and dogs coming into their care.

"The strays and wandering dogs is about the same, but really abandonment and surrenders are higher because the cost of living has gone up so much," Ms Debenham said.

" People are struggling to support the pets they've got. "

Ms Debenham said there could be 70 to 120 animals at SAFE at any time.

Anyone who comes across an injured or abused animal is urged to contact the RSPCA on 1300 CRUELTY or 1300 278 358.

World.title: The healthcare change that has some veterans furious
World.content:
In the Senate on Wednesday, Jacqui Lambie rose to speak on an extraordinarily personal topic — her recent surgery for vaginal prolapse.

She told the parliament of her challenges in seeking the surgery through the Department of Veterans Affairs (DVA), and her eventual decision to pay for the surgery out of her own pocket.

"If I was like the majority of female veterans, I would have had to wait for DVA to approve my claim," she said.

"And then I would have to search, and hope, and hope, that there would be a gynaecologist that would accept the low rate paid by DVA.

"That's how much they care about our vaginas."

Senator Lambie was visibly emotional when she described her health challenges. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

She linked her personal experience to the concerns being expressed by other veterans about looming changes to how the DVA manages access to allied healthcare.

From the middle of next year, a $5,000 threshold will be introduced for veterans spending on allied healthcare.

The government is quick to point out that it is not a cap. But spending over $5,000 will be subject to new scrutiny to determine if it is "clinically effective".

Senator Lambie's specific situation was not related to the changes, but she said the threshold could have harmed her ability to seek physiotherapy post-surgery.

Matt Keogh says he wants little real-world impact on veterans as a result of the changes. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The government is now facing substantial pressure over its plans, and was not helped when Veterans Affairs Minister Matt Keogh told the parliament he "got it wrong" after initially declining a meeting with veterans concerned about the threshold.

Government sources suggest questions around the threshold are being considered at the highest levels, including up to the prime minister's office.

What's changing?

The $5,000 threshold was first announced in May's budget.

It was described as an "annual monetary limit for veterans' allied health services" that would save the budget roughly $750 million over three years and $340 million each year after that.

The threshold aims to limit what the government describes as "overservicing" — where there is no clinical justification for the volume of appointments and services provided.

Veterans have access to various healthcare benefits covered by the government, including allied health care depending on injuries or conditions resulting from their service.

NT veterans join calls for health funding cap removal The federal government wants to cap access to health supports to $5,000 a year for injured war veterans, but there are growing concerns some will be worse-off as a result.

Department figures suggest that only around 10 per cent of veteran cardholders spend more than $5,000 on allied health services each year.

A Senate estimates hearing in June heard examples of overcharging that the department said it was keen to tackle.

In one case, a single patient was charged $101,000 in a single year by a dietitian, equating to 19 appointments a week.

Another veteran was charged $47,000 in a year for podiatry.

Department officials pointed to these as extreme examples of what it considered to be overservicing.

Its answer is the $5,000 threshold — granting funds to that amount but charges beyond would be subject to a "demonstrated clinical need".

Finding a fix

Both the department and minister, Matt Keogh, have pointed to a long period of planned consultation to run before the changes take effect.

There is a stated desire to ensure there is no service gap — that is, when veterans hit the $5,000 threshold they are not barred from accessing services they need while paperwork is processed.

But exactly how that will work is not yet clear.

The government has pointed to its process of consultation as its means of working out answers to questions like how clinical need will be measured, who needs to prove it (the veteran or provider) and what happens if DVA determines that clinical need does not exist.

Jacqui Lambie has a question for male ministers This week Jacqui Lambie shared her health struggles while the government and Coalition were busy making deals and One Nation launched a debate about cigarettes.

But that has raised the concerns of veterans' advocate groups, many of whom are fiercely protesting the changes.

Llani Kennealy from Women Veterans Australia said setting the threshold at all sent the wrong message to veterans seeking care.

"Imposing the cap automatically makes the veteran community feel like we were doing something wrong, seeking treatment for conditions as a result of our service," she said.

And she argued it would have an immediate impact should it be introduced.

"I have concerns about people delaying care, not accessing care, worrying — not all veterans are capable or particularly in the mental state to go on MyGov and assess where they're at with their treatment," she said.

"So it has a huge impact on the veteran community, and quite frankly, it's just the government putting the burden on the veterans to go after the shonky operators that have been over-servicing the veteran community."

Under repeated questioning on the issue in parliament this week, the veterans affairs minister pointed to changes the government was making to try to improve access to allied health.

Phillip Thompson says the government's actions do not stack up to its words. (Supplied: Australian of the Year)

These include increasing fees paid to providers to try to encourage more to take on veterans as clients and removing requirements for referrals.

Mr Keogh said the government wanted its introduction to have as little real-world impact on veterans as possible.

"What we have always been very clear about … is that we would always ensure that there was continuity of access, and that we would engage with all of the veteran community in relation to how we made sure that we maintained that good access," he said.

The shadow minister for defence personnel, Phil Thompson, said the cap had to go.

"The Albanese Labor government talks about supporting veterans, but its actions tell a different story," said the former soldier, who served in Afghanistan.

"This cap puts access to vital treatment at risk for veterans dealing with physical injuries, mental health challenges and service-related trauma."

World.title: Multiple child abuse reports ignored before boy's death in skip bin
World.content:
The coronial inquest into the death of a 13-year-old Port Lincoln boy who died after being tipped into a rubbish truck has wrapped up its first week of hearings.

WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

The court heard numerous Child Abuse Report Line reports (e-CARLs) had been made about him in the months leading up to his death.

Budda Spencer, as his family would like him to be known, died on May 11, 2021, after the skip bin he and two other boys, aged 11 and 12, were sleeping in was emptied into a rubbish truck.

The other two boys, who were under the Department for Child Protection's (DCP) care, were not harmed.

Naomi Kereru is presiding over the coronial inquest into the death of Budda Spencer. (ABC News)

The trio had spent the previous night in the grandstand of a local oval and decided they would all leave and stay together.

This week's inquest before deputy state coroner Naomi Kereru heard evidence from support agency staff and police at Port Lincoln Courthouse.

The court heard Budda Spencer's mother, Deborah Betts, made multiple reports to various agencies about her concerns relating to her son and that she was having trouble making him stay at home.

It also heard that three e-CARL reports were made about the boy in the month leading up to his death.

Those were made by Port Lincoln Brevet Sergeant Maddison Sellick, who phoned in two of the reports to make sure the DCP actioned them — which they had not done to her knowledge.

The first week of the inquest was heard at Port Lincoln Courthouse. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Brevet Sergeant Sellick told the coronial inquest one report was lodged when she learned Budda stayed at an address known to police as a drug use and distribution house.

"That address was a very active drug address and it concerned me [Budda] was around drug use and drug distribution," Brevet Sargeant Sellick said.

The second e-CARL notice was made after a breach of Budda's bail curfew and a police search detected cannabis in his shoes.

"The man that Budda Spencer said himself and the boys had obtained the cannabis from was someone that police were very aware of," Brevet Sergeant Sellick told the inquest.

"It was a male that intelligence suggested at the time would give and receive illicit drugs in exchange for sexual favours.

"There was nothing to suggest that it was happening at the time, but it gave a feeling of concern that perhaps the boys might be of risk of it in the future."

Budda Spencer's mother and maternal grandmother leaving a coronial inquest on Monday. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Brevet Sergeant Sellick made a third e-CARL report on May 6, five days before Budda's death, after his mother Deborah Betts told her she could not control him and said: "There is nothing I can do for him anymore."

The court heard Budda was on bail for various offences but ended up in custody because he did not want to return to his grandmother's home where his family was staying.

Brevet Sergeant Sellick said she did not think Budda understood his bail agreement, curfew or court proceedings, leading to him spending four days at the Youth Training Centre in Adelaide.

Budda Spencer was killed in an incident involving an industrial bin at Port Lincoln in 2021. (Supplied)

The court earlier heard he had a hearing disability and had been diagnosed with learning delays.

Brevet Sergeant Sellick filed an Identified Charge Sequencing Report to record that Budda was living in a poorly supported home environment with little to no supervision on May 6.

"DCP still have no active case for this child," the report stated.

Police alert child services

Appearing on Thursday, SAPOL Crime Prevention Sergeant First Class Dianne Baker-Tagg told the court she emailed the Port Lincoln DCP manager Ellen Lodge on April 30.

She outlined concerns about Budda's welfare but received no response.

Sergeant First Class Di Baker-Tagg arriving at Port Lincoln Courthouse on Thursday morning. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Another team member attended a Vulnerable Families Framework meeting on May 4 to raise the same concerns at a fortnightly meeting with agencies. There was no DCP representative at that meeting.

Counsel for SAPOL Ben Garnaut questioned Sergeant Baker-Tagg about the staffing at the DCP office.

"You made the observation of a degree on ongoing instability in the Port Lincoln DCP office and that the manager position was being filled by fly-in, fly-out staff," he said.

Sergeant Baker-Tagg said DCP staff in Port Lincoln advised her that they were understaffed and had restraints.

She said the manager position was now filled.

Complex inter-agency triaging

The former manager of Port Lincoln's Aboriginal Family Support Services (AFSS), Angela Backman, told the inquest on Tuesday there were complex traumas involved in the children that were referred to their organisation.

Angela Backman was a former manager of Port Lincoln's Aboriginal Family Support Services. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Ms Backman said DCP would close a child's case once they referred them to agencies that would engage the families in programs to improve parenting for better outcomes for the children.

However, the programs were voluntary, and the agencies did not have statutory powers to force parents or caregivers to attend.

If families did not attend the programs, the agency would close their case and make an e-CARL report so that DCP would then open a new case to consider.

There were inter-agency fortnightly meetings under the Vulnerable Families Framework in Port Lincoln involving SAPOL, DCP, local schools and support agencies.

One of these services was West Coast Youth and Community Services (WCYCS).

Port Lincoln Courthouse was the setting for the first week of hearings into the death of Budda Spencer. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

WCYCS senior youth worker Tony Perks told the inquest the meetings discussed and coordinated approaches for children at risk.

Budda had been tabled at a meeting in early May, and a decision was made for Budda to have one-on-one mentoring with an Aboriginal youth worker from WCYCS.

Mr Perks said while DCP was a member of the Vulnerable Families Framework, their attendance was sporadic and they were not at the May meeting.

The inquest continues in Adelaide on Monday for a week to hear evidence from DCP and Department of Human Services staff, before adjourning until October 20 for four days.

World.title: 'Horrific consequences': Aussie star almost hit by car in Tour of Britain
World.content:
Australian cyclist Maeve Plouffe has revealed she nearly got hit by a car while riding in this week's Tour of Britain — and has warned of potentially more "horrific consequences" for a sport already reeling from tragedy.

Plouffe, the 27-year-old former Sydney track star who grabbed Commonwealth team pursuit gold and individual silver in 2022, prompted organisers of the week-long road race to review safety procedures after she outlined her "scary" experience.

Plouffe had to withdraw from the race, having suffered a puncture during the opening stage in Cumbria on Wednesday, and her revelation on Instagram about an alarming episode with a car as she attempted to chase back to the peloton.

Plouffe posted the statement of her close call on her personal Instagram account. (Instagram/@maeveplouffe)

Her comments came only days after British rider Finlay Tarling died last week during stage eight of the Volta a Portugal after he was hit by a non-race light goods vehicle that had entered the course.

Explaining her withdrawal, Plouffe added: "While the race convoy was still in sight, and I was less than two minutes down, there were cars from the general public coming at me from all directions, including one that nearly hit me on a roundabout.

"Later on, the moto escort was wonderful, and I felt much safer.

"But considering the recent devastating events in our cycling community, it's scary to see situations like this, when we know that this can have horrific consequences, especially so soon after suffering such a tragedy."

She was referring to the death of the 19-year-old Tarling, who was killed last week in a high-speed collision with a van, which had strayed onto the road during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

British rider Finlay Tarling (right) was killed by a non-race light goods vehicle during the Volta a Portugal last week. (Getty Images: Huw Fairclough)

Before the Tour of Britain Women had begun, an emotional tribute was paid to Tarling, with his picture projected onto a large screen while all 114 riders and roadside fans joined in a minute's applause to honour him.

Tarling was the younger brother of Netcompany Ineos rider Josh Tarling, who will ride the Vuelta a España Grand Tour, which begins on Saturday, in honour of his sibling.

Organisers have swiftly taken note of Plouffe with Jonathan Day, events director of British Cycling Ventures — the commercial arm of British Cycling that organises the Tour — saying in a statement: "We're taking those comments extremely seriously."

"Rider safety is paramount and will always be treated as a priority in our planning and how we operate any race.

"We're reviewing what happened with Maeve and her team, O'Shea Red Chilli Bikes, with the seriousness and empathy these comments demand.

"We recognise this comes at an especially difficult time for the cycling community, so we want to reassure all riders, teams and fans of the sport at this time of how seriously we are treating these comments."

The race continued on Thursday with Dutch superstar Lorena Wiebes claiming her second successive stage victory between Clitheroe and Blackpool but only after that second stage had been neutralised because of a car accident.

Australian rider Georgia Baker, fresh from her golden Commonwealth Games on the track in Glasgow, was also caught up in a crash on the route.

Wiebes is 14 seconds ahead of Italy's Chiara Consonni (Canyon-SRAM zondacrypto) in the general classification as the race moves into Wales on Friday.

AAP

World.title: Missing hiker Lily Hooper's body recovered from NSW bush, police say
World.content:
The body of hiker Lily Hooper has been recovered from dense bushland in the NSW Southern Highlands more than a week after she went missing.

A NSW Police spokesperson said the body was retrieved from bushland in Nattai National Park last night after an eight-day multi-agency search.

Ms Hooper's body was located about 11:30am on Thursday, but Assistant Commissioner Joseph Cassar said flying it out proved difficult due to the rough terrain.

Lily Hooper, 18, went missing while hiking in the Nattai National Park. (Supplied: NSW Police)

"We are exploring every opportunity to get Lily out of there," he said on Thursday afternoon.

A NSW Police spokesperson said this morning the body was retrieved last night and would undergo a post-mortem examination.

Ms Hooper left her home in south-western Sydney on the morning of Wednesday, August 12, to go hiking in the Nattai National Park, 90 kilometres south-west of Sydney.

Her family alerted police after she failed to return home that evening, which sparked a multi-agency search effort to locate her.

Her car was later found at the beginning of the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail, a challenging 16 kilometre track for more advanced hikers.

Almost 100 members of the Australian Defence Force helped with the search for Lily Hooper. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Almost 1,000 people , working day and night, helped search for Ms Hooper, including almost 100 Australian Defence Force personnel, 280 NSW SES volunteers and specialist police crews.

The search included scouring dense undergrowth, complex cliff lines and deep ravines, and crews were forced to deal with inclement weather that hampered their efforts.

The Nattai National park has dense bushland, deep ravines and high cliffs. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Despite this, no sign of the 18-year-old or any personal belongings were located until Thursday.

NSW Premier Chris Minns was informed during budget estimates that Ms Hooper had been found, initially saying that she was alive.

This was widely reported by Australian media, including the ABC.

Mr Minns later told a parliamentary hearing that a body had been found.

SES volunteers stand at the command post where the search for Lily Hooper was coordinated. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

The body was found by an SES searcher and there was an "eight to 10-minute" period when Ms Hooper's family believed she was found alive, according to police.

Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon later "unreservedly" apologised for the "miscommunication" and "any additional trauma" to Ms Hooper's family.

World.title: Live: US markets down amid plan to 'collapse' Iran's economy, ASX to follow
World.content:
Bitcoin has surged 5% overnight, boosted by positive policy signals in the US.

On the back of that, cryptocurrency-related stocks rocketed too, a day after the US Treasury Department said it would support more long-duration bonds, boosting risk assets, and as US President Donald Trump urged Congress to pass legislation establishing clear rules for digital assets.

The Treasury's move to double buyback sizes for long-duration debt came after a major bond selloff pushed the 30-year Treasury yield to its highest level since 2007. Higher yields are typically a negative for risk assets like cryptocurrencies because they increase the returns on safer investments.

While the Treasury's intervention was relatively small and offered only short-lived relief for bonds, it nevertheless provided a positive signal for crypto, analysts said.

Here's a a research note from Alex Kuptsikevich, chief market analyst at brokerage FxPro:

"The rally (in crypto) was then fueled by a wave of short-covering, following weeks of extremely narrow trading."

Bitcoin was last up 3.48% at $71,505, having crossed the $70,000 mark for the first time since June.

The world's largest cryptocurrency has lost about 18% so far this year and remains down about 43% from its record high in October.

Investors may also have been encouraged by Trump's show of support for crypto legislation, the industry's top policy priority.

Trump, who promised on the campaign trail to make the United States the "crypto capital of the world" and who has profited from his own crypto ventures, on Wednesday called on lawmakers at a White House event with crypto executives to pass a "fair version of the Clarity Act," currently stalled in the Senate.

More, from US Tiger Securities analyst Bo Pei:

"Trump's comments (on Wednesday) are incrementally positive because they suggest the White House is putting more direct pressure on Congress to get the legislation done."

The Clarity Act, if enacted, would define whether cryptocurrency qualifies as a security or a commodity, clarifying jurisdiction between the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission over the sector.

Industry ​executives and analysts have said that without legislation, regulations are vulnerable to shifting political winds and court challenges.

However, many Democrats, and some Republicans, say they would not support a bill without strong language banning political officials, including Trump, from profiting from their own crypto ventures.

Trump disclosed more than $1.4 billion in earnings from his family's crypto ventures in 2025.

Ether gained 2.46% and was last trading at $2,272, its highest level in over three months.

- With Reuters

World.title: Alcaraz confirms US Open return amid record prize money reveal
World.content:
Carlos Alcaraz is set to return to action at the US Open, ending four months of injury torment, and will be back competing for a record grand slam winner's prize of $US5.5 million ($7.7 million) in New York.

The news of the seven-time grand slam winner's comeback at Flushing Meadows will be music to the ears of former Australian Open boss Craig Tiley, who has been able to begin his reign in charge of the US Open by announcing unprecedented riches to the players.

Seven-time grand slam champion Alcaraz has not played since April due to a concerning wrist injury.

He announced his return on Thursday in unusual fashion, with the help of football journalist Fabrizio Romano.

Romano, who is usually breaking news of big football transfers, used his catchphrase, "Here we go," to announce Alcaraz's return on Instagram, while the reigning champ repeated the message on X.

Alcaraz, who started the year by winning the Australian Open, has not played since withdrawing from the Barcelona Open in April. He has missed both the ‌French Open and ⁠Wimbledon while his great rival, Jannik Sinner, has largely dominated.

Now he is fit to return to the scene of his first grand slam triumph in 2022, when he became the youngest man to reach world number one in the rankings.

Alcaraz's return is fantastic news for Tiley, the former Tennis Australia CEO who has taken up the equivalent job at the US Tennis Association (USTA) and has been able to announce an overall prize fund of $US108 million — the first time the $US100m barrier has been broken at a slam.

Alcaraz's 2026 season has been cruelled by a wrist injury. (Getty Images: Quality Sport Images/Alvaro Medranda)

It is the biggest prize pot in the sport's history and represents a 20 per cent rise for the second consecutive year.

"This is a significant first step in a multi-year investment in athletes as the US Open continues to be the best economic opportunity for players and the most valuable platform in tennis for players, fans and partners," Tiley said.

"We are proud to deliver record-setting prize money and expanded player benefits as well as providing a new platform to work together with players."

That platform is the formation of a Grand Slam Player Council, which is intended to give players a voice on a range of issues such as prize money.

Organisers hope all this will ward off the kind of player protests that occurred at the French Open and Wimbledon.

The champions' winning cheque will be $US5.5 million, up from the $5 million that Sabalenka and Alcaraz won last year.

Players will earn $US140,000 just for making it into the main draw, while a quarterfinalist earns $US780,000, a semifinalist $US1.45 million and runners-up $US2.8 million.

Meanwhile, there was good news for the Australian challenge following the withdrawal of Spain's Alejandro Davidovich Fokina from the main draw through injury.

It meant Alexei Popyrin was able to be advanced to the main draw and the reciprocal wildcard he had been given by the USTA could instead go to his Australian teammate Dane Sweeny, who will make his Flushing Meadows debut at 25.

That takes the current Australian contingent set to start the action on August 30 to a total of 14 — eight men and six women — with more attempting to make it through next week's qualifying.

AAP

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Albanese admits regret over podcast for the first time; Woman at centre of Sydney Swans allegation breaks silence
World.content:
Washington: The Asia-based USS George Washington aircraft carrier is now operating in the Middle East, relieving a long-deployed carrier following reports of mental health challenges and supply shortages aboard while it was supporting the Iran war.



US Central Command said on social media that the carrier arrived in the region on Wednesday. It was not clear when the USS Abraham Lincoln would arrive back in the United States, or whether it would make a port stop along the way, but the journey takes just over a month.

Sailors and marines line the deck of aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln as it deploys from San Diego. K.C. Alfred/The San Diego Union-Tribune via AP

The Washington arrived as concerns have grown about the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment, which has included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 250 days, and about reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products.



Several Democratic lawmakers have pressed the Department of Defence for accountability over conditions aboard the Lincoln, which Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said were “completely misrepresented”.

US President Donald Trump this week played down reports about conditions on the Lincoln, which left its home port in San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January.



Extended deployments of carriers wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.



While hostilities between the US and Iran have calmed in recent weeks, the US Navy is enforcing a reimposed blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz.



AP

World.title: Body of bushwalker retrieved from Southern Highlands bushland
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWTragedy Body of bushwalker retrieved from Southern Highlands bushland Daniel Lo Surdo Updated August 21, 2026 — 8:47am ,first published 7:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The body of 18-year-old bushwalker Lily Hooper has been recovered from dense bushland in the NSW Southern Highlands, hours after it was discovered by a search and rescue team following an eight-day search. The body was retrieved after 6pm on Thursday, a police source confirmed to the Herald. Friends, family and loved ones of Sydney bushwalker Lily Hooper have been grieving her loss, having initially heard she was found alive. Kate Geraghty The body was discovered in scrub in the Nattai National Park by an SES rescuer about 11.30am on Thursday. Initial reports from the rescuers led to confusion about whether Hooper was alive, before updated information conveyed to the search operation’s command post confirmed she had died. An autopsy to determine the circumstances and cause of Hooper’s death is expected to take place in the coming days, but could begin on Friday. Formal identification will also occur soon.



Related Article Tragedy How a family, police and politicians were wrongly told about bushwalker’s survival NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon has shouldered the blame for the communication error that led to the belief Hooper was alive. The incorrect information was passed to Premier Chris Minns, who announced to a budget estimates committee that Hooper had been found alive on Thursday, just to withdraw the news minutes later. “I unashamedly apologise for any additional trauma that may have caused Lily’s family,” Lanyon said on Thursday. “The miscommunication obviously was born out of elation that Lily had been found, and her condition at that time was such that searchers were relieved … Tragically, that miscommunication then led to a deflation.”



Hundreds of searchers had scoured dense bush in the national park looking for Hooper since she was reported missing on August 12. She had left her Oakdale home in Sydney’s south-west that morning to hike the Bonnum Pic walking trail, a strenuous, rugged track with limited phone signal. The beginning of the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail. Kate Geraghty The rescue personnel included members of the Australian Defence Force, police riding on horseback and motorbikes, firefighters, national park rangers, paramedics and SES volunteers. Police helicopters and drones also scoured the national park from the air. Lanyon had spoken to NSW SES Commissioner Mike Wassing and said he would review the communication failure, he told reporters on Thursday. “This is not a circumstance I would like to see repeated,” Lanyon said.



Minns apologised on Thursday for sharing the false information, saying he “genuinely believed” he was sharing positive news. “I am profoundly sorry to think that anything I said may have added to their heartbreak at an already devastating time,” the premier said. More to come. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Hayden Panettiere’s boyfriend Brian Hickerson makes first public comments over death
World.content:
CultureCelebrityVale Hayden Panettiere’s boyfriend Brian Hickerson makes first public comments over death Nell Geraets Updated August 21, 2026 — 8:07am ,first published 12:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hayden Panettiere’s on-again, off-again boyfriend Brian Hickerson has made his first public comments following the star’s death earlier this week. Hickerson and his brother Zach were both in the apartment complex where the actor went into cardiac arrest and died according to police reports. Hayden Panettiere’s on-and-off-again boyfriend Brian Hickerson was with her when she died. Getty “Hayden’s death remains under investigation and it is important to allow that investigation to proceed,” Hickerson’s lawyer said in a statement provided to US outlet TMZ overnight Thursday (AEST). “As has been publicly reported, police confirmed there were no signs of foul play … Out of respect for Hayden’s loved ones and the ongoing investigation, there will be no further comment at this time,” the statement said.



The Greenville Police Department confirmed on Tuesday (US time), via a heavily redacted report, that it was the Hickerson brothers who made the 911 call over the weekend. Related Article Updated

Vale Nashville star Hayden Panettiere dies at age 36 Hickerson, who dated Panettiere on-and-off from 2018, reportedly “did not become emotional” until paramedics officially declared her dead. He spoke with the police about the actor, and showed them “a bag of medications” she had been taking, according to the police report. The names of the medications were redacted. Hickerson and his brother Zach – who Panettiere also reportedly dated in 2019 – have not been accused of any involvement in Panettiere’s death. A preliminary investigation did not indicate any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances, and the Greenville County Coroner’s Office reported no signs of trauma that would have contributed to her death. The case is still under investigation, and the official cause and manner of Panettiere’s death remains pending. A lawyer who has represented Hickerson was contacted for comment.



Hickerson’s presence at the scene has brought his turbulent relationship with Panettiere back into the spotlight. The actor detailed several instances of abuse by Hickerson in her memoir This Is Me: A Reckoning, released in May. The relationship appeared to end in 2020 amid the allegations. During recent interviews to promote her memoir, Panettiere even recounted her efforts to distance herself from an abusive boyfriend. “Abusers – they weave themselves like weeds into your life,” she said on a podcast in May. Following her death, Panettiere’s estranged mother Lesley Vogel told US outlets that Panettiere was trying to distance herself from Hickerson, but she “lost her way”. “This person in her life that we have been trying to get rid of for quite some time was with her at her death, and that was Brian Hickerson,” Vogel told NBC News this week. “I think Hayden sadly lost her way, and I wish it were different … I wish she had stayed true to herself because she had many incredible attributes.” Police attended the home of Hickerson’s family on Wednesday (US time), just days after Panettiere went into cardiac arrest. However, the Greenville Police Department said this was a welfare check, and it did not relate to the investigation into the actor’s death. No incident report was required.



Who is Brian Hickerson? Hickerson is a 37-year-old aspiring actor from South Carolina. His romantic relationship with Panettiere reportedly began in 2018 when they met in West Hollywood. According to Panettiere, their entanglement progressed rapidly, with the pair spending most of their time together, largely unbeknownst to Panettiere’s family members. The pair were first linked in 2018, but went on to have a turbulent on-and-off-again relationship with multiple alleged incidents of domestic violence. Getty However, the Heroes actor details multiple instances in which Hickerson abused her in her memoir. During one particular instance, she said he beat her so badly that she did not leave the house for weeks. Panettiere notes in her book that she did not report the abuse to police to prevent the public from finding out. According to People magazine, Hickerson was arrested on a domestic violence charge in May 2019, and was charged with felony domestic violence in May. This was then dismissed in September.



Related Article Analysis

Celebrity life Young stars are thrown into fame and riches. But the spotlight can be deadly On Valentine’s Day in 2020, Panettiere wrote that a night of drinking turned violent when Hickerson pushed her into a wall and slapped her. According to The New York Times, police responded to a call about a disturbance and Hickerson spent the night in jail. He was charged with seven felony counts, including assault, injuring a spouse or partner, dissuading a witness from prosecuting a crime, and misdemeanour battery. He pleaded no contest to two felony counts of injuring Panettiere. Hickerson subsequently served a short amount of time in jail, and was sentenced to four years of probation, anger management and Alcoholics Anonymous sessions (which, according to Hickerson, are led by actor Shia LaBeouf). These requirements have since been fulfilled, and Hickerson recently worked with his legal representative to try and reduce his conviction to misdemeanours. These requests, one of which was made as recently as last week, have so far been denied.



Have they been together since? Panettiere and Hickerson were seen together several times since the charges were placed. The pair were seen having a physical fight outside a bar in Los Angeles in 2022, according to People. “None of it is okay, and I want to make sure that everybody knows that,” Panettiere told the magazine at the time. “But I am open to people who are willing to get help and make amends. He’s gone to treatment and done his time. And I’m trying to live in a place of forgiveness.” Hayden Panettiere and Brian Hickerson both attended the funeral of Panettiere’s brother in 2023. GC Images Hickerson also attended the funeral of Panettiere’s brother Jansen, who died from an enlarged heart in 2023.



The pair were seen together as recently as March 2026, when they were spotted at the Los Angeles Airport. However, according to The New York Times, Panettiere hired private security that same month to help keep Hickerson away. What did Panettiere say about their relationship? In 2022, Panettiere shared her thoughts on their relationship with People. “It was a very dark and complicated time in my life. But a lot of women go through what I went through, and I want people to know it’s okay to ask for help,” she said. Related Article Vale Overdose suspected in Hayden Panettiere death as emergency audio emerges “I am trying to live in a place of understanding. I think [Hickerson] has done his time and was willing to get help. I think about the things I have done in my life that people forgave me for. Making amends is a really important thing that you learn in treatment. And it gives you a lot of inner peace.”



In her memoir, Panettiere was open about her own struggles with alcohol addiction and substance abuse. In 2015, she checked herself into a treatment facility to get professional help for postpartum depression, and in early 2020, she entered an in-patient treatment centre for alcohol and opioid addiction. She also expressed how she felt while Hickerson was serving time in jail. “I needed him to admit his wrongs and change because of them, but I didn’t want to traumatise him in an irreversible way,” she wrote. World.content:
NationalQueenslandCrime Man charged with rape, stalking after alleged morning attack on woman Courtney Kruk and Julius Dennis August 21, 2026 — 7:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 32-year-old man has been charged with rape and stalking after the alleged “horrific” assault of a young woman on her early-morning walk west of Brisbane. Detectives from the Ferny Grove Child Protection and Investigation Unit allege the woman, in her 20s, was walking along Brookfield Road near Moggill Creek in Brookfield, a semi-rural suburb west of Brisbane, about 6.33am on Thursday when she was stopped by an unknown man. Police say the Raceview man sexually assaulted the woman before she fought him off and escaped, running up the creek towards the Brookfield Showgrounds. There was a heavy police presence in Brookfield on Thursday. NINE He was described as wearing black shorts and a black jumper, and police said he fled on foot following the attack.



Detective Superintendent Andrew Massingham described the alleged assault as “horrific” and said it had shocked the local community. “She was a determined young lady that knew what was occurring to her was horrific. “She knew help was some distance away, but she was very lucky to make it through up an adjoining creek up towards the showgrounds at Brookfield, where she called for assistance, and that assistance was provided very quickly,” he said. “I know this incident has shocked not only the local community but also the wider Brisbane region.”



The woman was taken to the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital for treatment. Officers found a 32-year-old man on Moons Lane, a street in Brookfield, on Thursday afternoon, and took him into custody. He has been charged with six counts of rape, stalking, assault with intent to commit rape, assault occasioning bodily harm and deprivation of liberty. An investigation command centre had been established in Ferny Grove, with a mobile beat set up at the showgrounds. Nine News He was expected to appear before Brisbane’s Magistrates Court on Friday.



A heavy police presence was noted near the bridge and throughout Brookfield on Thursday. Massingham told reporters he expected officers would have spoken to more than 100 people by Friday morning. An investigation command centre had been established in Ferny Grove, Massingham said, adding a mobile beat would be set up at the showgrounds. He appealed for anyone who was in the Brookfield area about the time of the alleged assault to get in touch with police. “It is imperative that any person in that area between 5.30am and 7.30am comes forward with any information relating to any suspicious activity or any dashcam that they may have of that general area,” Massingham said.

World.title: ‘Heinous’ crime: China’s disgraced king of real estate sentenced to life in jail
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCrime ‘Heinous’ crime: China’s disgraced king of real estate sentenced to life in jail Bloomberg News August 21, 2026 — 6:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

China Evergrande Group’s founder Hui Ka Yan has been sentenced to life in prison, bringing an end to one of the most dramatic rise and fall stories in China’s corporate history. The disgraced property tycoon, once Asia’s second-richest man, had turned Evergrande into a poster child of corporate excess during China’s long real estate boom. But after his empire came crashing down following a 2021 default, he was caught in a dragnet of official investigations that ultimately caused his downfall. Hui Ka Yan was sentenced alongside 56 others involved in Evergrande, including his sons Xu Zhijian and Xu Tenghe. undefined/Xinhua via AP Hui, who appeared visibly aged in court with greying hair, was sentenced alongside 56 others involved in Evergrande, including his sons Xu Zhijian and Xu Tenghe. His assets will be confiscated, and his companies were fined a combined 15.82 billion yuan ($3.3 billion). The move draws a curtain on what for years was one of China’s great success stories. Hui had binged on debt during Evergrande’s expansion, turning it into the world’s most indebted developer as he transformed the property giant into a sprawling conglomerate.



But Chinese authorities concluded that his rise was built on deception. They said Hui had perpetrated a massive financial fraud that included inflating assets and concealing liabilities. Related Article Opinion

Inside China China’s property cancer is spreading through its economy Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In 2017, Hui had a net worth of $US45.3 billion ($63.3 billiion), the highest in Asia, according to Forbes. By 2023, it had shrunk to an estimated $US3 billion. On Thursday, the court in Shenzhen ordered the confiscation of all his personal property. In April, Hui had pleaded guilty in a Chinese court to charges including illegally taking public deposits and fundraising fraud. “The amount involved in the crime is exceptionally large, the circumstances are particularly heinous, exceptionally heavy economic losses have been caused, and the harm to society is extremely grave,” a report from state media outlet Xinhua wrote, adding that Evergrande and Hui “must be severely punished in accordance with the law.”



Evergrande and Hui were also found guilty of fraudulently issuing securities, violating information disclosure rules as well as bribery. Meanwhile, the founder was accused of embezzling company assets through dividend mechanisms. The sentence doesn’t bring an end to the numerous legal fights surrounding Evergrande. The company is now in liquidation, with an army of creditors inside and outside of China poring over its assets in the hopes of recovering some of their heavy losses. During its prime, Evergrande built more than 1300 projects across 280 cities. Bloomberg Rags to riches Hui, also known as Xu Jiayin in Mandarin, was born in Henan province in 1958 and grew up in poverty. Encouraged by the prospect of Deng Xiaoping’s economic reform plan, the son of a wood cutter quit his job at a steel firm in 1992 and later began developing property in Guangzhou, the provincial capital of Guangdong. He then founded Evergrande in 1996 and rode the wave of China’s unprecedented real estate boom.



Evergrande, which means “permanence and greatness” in Chinese, relied on heavy borrowing to fuel its growth, becoming the largest dollar-debt borrower among its peers and for a time the country’s biggest developer by sales. During its prime, the firm built more than 1300 projects across 280 cities. Supercharged by real estate riches, it also expanded its reach into industries ranging from bottled water to professional soccer and electric vehicles. For a long time, Evergrande skirted liquidity scares by tapping tycoons in China and Hong Kong to buy the firm’s stock and bonds. Hui also turned to his own suppliers and retail investors for financial backing. But Beijing’s crackdown on the property sector since 2020 capped its borrowing capacity, effectively cutting Hui off from credit markets. Hui’s charges follow a long list of harsh actions by Chinese authorities against corporate magnates. The sentence doesn’t bring an end to the numerous legal fights surrounding Evergrande. The company is now in liquidation, with an army of creditors inside and outside of China poring over its assets in the hopes of recovering some of their heavy losses. Anbang Group’s former chairman, Wu Xiaohui, was sentenced to 18 years in prison for fraud and embezzlement in 2018. That same year, China Huarong Asset Management Co. Chairman Lai Xiaomin was arrested amid a corruption scandal before being executed in 2021 on charges including bribery. HNA Group chairman Chen Feng was detained a few months later along with chief executive officer Tan Xiangdong for unspecified crimes.



Evergrande defaulted on its debt in late 2021. Following failed restructuring attempts, it was given a winding up order in Hong Kong in 2024, marking a significant escalation in the unravelling of the sector. Later that year, a mainland Chinese court accepted a liquidation application filed against one of its major onshore units. Hui was taken away by Chinese police in 2023 and held under so-called residential surveillance — a type of police action that falls short of formal detention or arrest. Apart from a company filing confirming Hui being put under control, Chinese authorities had remained tight-lipped about his status since then. Related Article Opinion

Inside China The Chinese dream has turned into a nightmare In 2024, Chinese regulators accused Evergrande’s main onshore unit of inflating more than 560 billion yuan of revenue by recognising sales in advance, an alleged fraud that dwarfs that of Luckin Coffee and Enron. China then suspended the operations of PricewaterhouseCoopers, Evergrande’s long-time auditor, for six months and imposed fines. Much of Hui’s known wealth was derived from his controlling stake in Evergrande and the cash dividends he’s received from the company since its 2009 listing in Hong Kong. Hui had pocketed more than $US7 billion over the past decade, thanks to the firm’s generous payouts, according to Bloomberg calculations.

World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street declines as oil rises on escalating Middle East tensions
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street declines as oil rises on escalating Middle East tensions Stan Choe Updated August 21, 2026 — 6:12am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A rise in oil prices is sending worries about inflation and yields in the bond market higher, erasing some of the relief the US Treasury Department had created a day earlier. The higher yields and a big drop for Walmart helped to drag the US sharemarket lower. The S&P 500 fell 0.9 per cent for its fourth loss in the five days since setting its record last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1 per cent. Treasury yields climbed after the price of Brent crude rose 2.4 per cent following US President Donald Trump’s latest threat to Iran. Wall Street closed in the red for the fourth time in five days. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 4.55am AEST pointing to a fall of 23 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.3 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.10¢. Guzman y Gomez and Inghams are among the companies scheduled to report earnings today. The bond market remains the centre of the action after yields charged higher through the northern summer on worries about high inflation, gargantuan government debts and other factors. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent made a move that jolted financial markets to at least double the size of his department’s planned purchases of longer-term Treasurys from September 9 to November 4.



That helped to push yields down after the 10-year Treasury’s yield had hit its highest level in more than a year, and the 30-year yield got back to where it was in 2007, before the Great Recession sent yields towards zero worldwide. It’s a big deal because high yields slow the economy by raising interest payments for people, companies and the government, and they can undercut prices for shares and other investments. Related Article Opinion

GST The GST carve-up is cooked, but we need to stop piling onto WA Millie Muroi Economics Writer But analysts had cautioned the effect may be short-lived, given how small the purchases are relative to the overall size of the Treasury market and how they don’t fix the fundamental concerns of investors that had driven up yields in the first place. Plus, more signals arrived quickly to push worries higher. The US government’s debt topped $US40 trillion ($56.2 trillion) on Wednesday, a staggering record that arrived months after the national debt first blew past the $US39 trillion mark in April, because Washington continues to spend far more money than it brings in. And on Thursday, the price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 2 per cent to $US93.41 as uncertainty continues about when the war with Iran will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. Trump threatened Iran with “the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY” late on Wednesday, but provided few details.



That helped to push the 10-year Treasury yield up to 4.70 per cent from 4.65 per cent late on Wednesday. It’s almost back to its 4.71 per cent level from late Tuesday, before the Treasury Department made its announcement. A couple of encouraging reports on the US economy also helped to push up longer-term Treasury yields, which move with expectations for the economy and inflation in coming years. One said that fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week than economists had expected, while another said that manufacturing in the mid-Atlantic region appears to be much stronger than expected. On Wall Street, Walmart was one of the heaviest weights on the S&P 500 and fell 9.2 per cent even though it reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts had expected. Investors focused instead on how an important underlying measure of revenue growth at its stores slowed once more. Its forecast for profit in the current quarter also fell short of analysts’ expectations. Given its massive size, Walmart offers a look at how shoppers are doing across the United States. A surprisingly weak update on sales at US retailers overall last month had raised worries that shoppers may be succumbing to pressure from high inflation and a jobs market that may be looking less solid. Advance Auto Parts tumbled 24.6 per cent after the retailer reported weaker revenue for the latest quarter, even though its profit topped expectations. Chief executive Shane O’Kelly said that “tighter household budgets constrained spending more than we anticipated, especially during the last four weeks of the quarter”.



Spending by US consumers is the main engine of the economy, and a pullback by them could exacerbate what’s already a slowdown in growth for the economy. A pullback could also mean a double-whammy for travel companies, which would see fewer bookings when they have to pay higher prices for fuel. Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings fell 3.4 per cent, while United Airlines sank 3.5 per cent and American Airlines lost 2.5 per cent. Related Article Analysis

Trump's America Trump’s America faces a ‘doom loop’ as it falls in a $56 trillion hole Helping to keep Wall Street’s losses in check was Deere, which reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts had expected. It rose 6.9 per cent as the company said order trends indicate the agriculture equipment business looks set to accelerate after this year. Oil companies also rose with the gains for crude prices. Exxon Mobil added 0.8 per cent while ConocoPhillips climbed 3.3 per cent.



In sharemarkets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following a stronger finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi soared 5.9 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves after the two tech titans that dominate its market, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, jumped. Such swings have become more common for Seoul’s market, which has borne the brunt of rising and falling worries that winning stocks in the artificial-intelligence boom may have shot too high. Washington: The Asia-based USS George Washington aircraft carrier is now operating in the Middle East, relieving a long-deployed carrier following reports of mental health challenges and supply shortages aboard while it was supporting the Iran war.



US Central Command said on social media that the carrier arrived in the region on Wednesday. It was not clear when the USS Abraham Lincoln would arrive back in the United States, or whether it would make a port stop along the way, but the journey takes just over a month.

Sailors and marines line the deck of aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln as it deploys from San Diego. K.C. Alfred/The San Diego Union-Tribune via AP

The Washington arrived as concerns have grown about the Lincoln’s lengthy deployment, which has included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 250 days, and about reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products.



Several Democratic lawmakers have pressed the Department of Defence for accountability over conditions aboard the Lincoln, which Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said were “completely misrepresented”.

US President Donald Trump this week played down reports about conditions on the Lincoln, which left its home port in San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January.



Extended deployments of carriers wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.



While hostilities between the US and Iran have calmed in recent weeks, the US Navy is enforcing a reimposed blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: Body of bushwalker retrieved from Southern Highlands bushland
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWTragedy Body of bushwalker retrieved from Southern Highlands bushland Daniel Lo Surdo Updated August 21, 2026 — 8:47am ,first published 7:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The body of 18-year-old bushwalker Lily Hooper has been recovered from dense bushland in the NSW Southern Highlands, hours after it was discovered by a search and rescue team following an eight-day search. The body was retrieved after 6pm on Thursday, a police source confirmed to the Herald. Friends, family and loved ones of Sydney bushwalker Lily Hooper have been grieving her loss, having initially heard she was found alive. Kate Geraghty The body was discovered in scrub in the Nattai National Park by an SES rescuer about 11.30am on Thursday. Initial reports from the rescuers led to confusion about whether Hooper was alive, before updated information conveyed to the search operation’s command post confirmed she had died. An autopsy to determine the circumstances and cause of Hooper’s death is expected to take place in the coming days, but could begin on Friday. Formal identification will also occur soon.



Related Article Tragedy How a family, police and politicians were wrongly told about bushwalker’s survival NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon has shouldered the blame for the communication error that led to the belief Hooper was alive. The incorrect information was passed to Premier Chris Minns, who announced to a budget estimates committee that Hooper had been found alive on Thursday, just to withdraw the news minutes later. “I unashamedly apologise for any additional trauma that may have caused Lily’s family,” Lanyon said on Thursday. “The miscommunication obviously was born out of elation that Lily had been found, and her condition at that time was such that searchers were relieved … Tragically, that miscommunication then led to a deflation.”



Hundreds of searchers had scoured dense bush in the national park looking for Hooper since she was reported missing on August 12. She had left her Oakdale home in Sydney’s south-west that morning to hike the Bonnum Pic walking trail, a strenuous, rugged track with limited phone signal. The beginning of the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail. Kate Geraghty The rescue personnel included members of the Australian Defence Force, police riding on horseback and motorbikes, firefighters, national park rangers, paramedics and SES volunteers. Police helicopters and drones also scoured the national park from the air. Lanyon had spoken to NSW SES Commissioner Mike Wassing and said he would review the communication failure, he told reporters on Thursday. “This is not a circumstance I would like to see repeated,” Lanyon said.



Minns apologised on Thursday for sharing the false information, saying he “genuinely believed” he was sharing positive news. “I am profoundly sorry to think that anything I said may have added to their heartbreak at an already devastating time,” the premier said. World.title: Hayden Panettiere’s boyfriend Brian Hickerson makes first public comments over death
World.content:
CultureCelebrityVale Hayden Panettiere’s boyfriend Brian Hickerson makes first public comments over death Nell Geraets Updated August 21, 2026 — 8:07am ,first published 12:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hayden Panettiere’s on-again, off-again boyfriend Brian Hickerson has made his first public comments following the star’s death earlier this week. Hickerson and his brother Zach were both in the apartment complex where the actor went into cardiac arrest and died according to police reports. Hayden Panettiere’s on-and-off-again boyfriend Brian Hickerson was with her when she died. Getty “Hayden’s death remains under investigation and it is important to allow that investigation to proceed,” Hickerson’s lawyer said in a statement provided to US outlet TMZ overnight Thursday (AEST). “As has been publicly reported, police confirmed there were no signs of foul play … Out of respect for Hayden’s loved ones and the ongoing investigation, there will be no further comment at this time,” the statement said.



The Greenville Police Department confirmed on Tuesday (US time), via a heavily redacted report, that it was the Hickerson brothers who made the 911 call over the weekend. Related Article Updated

Vale Nashville star Hayden Panettiere dies at age 36 Hickerson, who dated Panettiere on-and-off from 2018, reportedly “did not become emotional” until paramedics officially declared her dead. He spoke with the police about the actor, and showed them “a bag of medications” she had been taking, according to the police report. The names of the medications were redacted. Hickerson and his brother Zach – who Panettiere also reportedly dated in 2019 – have not been accused of any involvement in Panettiere’s death. A preliminary investigation did not indicate any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances, and the Greenville County Coroner’s Office reported no signs of trauma that would have contributed to her death. The case is still under investigation, and the official cause and manner of Panettiere’s death remains pending. A lawyer who has represented Hickerson was contacted for comment.



Hickerson’s presence at the scene has brought his turbulent relationship with Panettiere back into the spotlight. The actor detailed several instances of abuse by Hickerson in her memoir This Is Me: A Reckoning, released in May. The relationship appeared to end in 2020 amid the allegations. During recent interviews to promote her memoir, Panettiere even recounted her efforts to distance herself from an abusive boyfriend. “Abusers – they weave themselves like weeds into your life,” she said on a podcast in May. Following her death, Panettiere’s estranged mother Lesley Vogel told US outlets that Panettiere was trying to distance herself from Hickerson, but she “lost her way”. “This person in her life that we have been trying to get rid of for quite some time was with her at her death, and that was Brian Hickerson,” Vogel told NBC News this week. “I think Hayden sadly lost her way, and I wish it were different … I wish she had stayed true to herself because she had many incredible attributes.” Police attended the home of Hickerson’s family on Wednesday (US time), just days after Panettiere went into cardiac arrest. However, the Greenville Police Department said this was a welfare check, and it did not relate to the investigation into the actor’s death. No incident report was required.



Who is Brian Hickerson? Hickerson is a 37-year-old aspiring actor from South Carolina. His romantic relationship with Panettiere reportedly began in 2018 when they met in West Hollywood. According to Panettiere, their entanglement progressed rapidly, with the pair spending most of their time together, largely unbeknownst to Panettiere’s family members. The pair were first linked in 2018, but went on to have a turbulent on-and-off-again relationship with multiple alleged incidents of domestic violence. Getty However, the Heroes actor details multiple instances in which Hickerson abused her in her memoir. During one particular instance, she said he beat her so badly that she did not leave the house for weeks. Panettiere notes in her book that she did not report the abuse to police to prevent the public from finding out. According to People magazine, Hickerson was arrested on a domestic violence charge in May 2019, and was charged with felony domestic violence in May. This was then dismissed in September.



Related Article Analysis

Celebrity life Young stars are thrown into fame and riches. But the spotlight can be deadly On Valentine’s Day in 2020, Panettiere wrote that a night of drinking turned violent when Hickerson pushed her into a wall and slapped her. According to The New York Times, police responded to a call about a disturbance and Hickerson spent the night in jail. He was charged with seven felony counts, including assault, injuring a spouse or partner, dissuading a witness from prosecuting a crime, and misdemeanour battery. He pleaded no contest to two felony counts of injuring Panettiere. Hickerson subsequently served a short amount of time in jail, and was sentenced to four years of probation, anger management and Alcoholics Anonymous sessions (which, according to Hickerson, are led by actor Shia LaBeouf). These requirements have since been fulfilled, and Hickerson recently worked with his legal representative to try and reduce his conviction to misdemeanours. These requests, one of which was made as recently as last week, have so far been denied.



Have they been together since? Panettiere and Hickerson were seen together several times since the charges were placed. The pair were seen having a physical fight outside a bar in Los Angeles in 2022, according to People. “None of it is okay, and I want to make sure that everybody knows that,” Panettiere told the magazine at the time. “But I am open to people who are willing to get help and make amends. He’s gone to treatment and done his time. And I’m trying to live in a place of forgiveness.” Hayden Panettiere and Brian Hickerson both attended the funeral of Panettiere’s brother in 2023. GC Images Hickerson also attended the funeral of Panettiere’s brother Jansen, who died from an enlarged heart in 2023.



The pair were seen together as recently as March 2026, when they were spotted at the Los Angeles Airport. However, according to The New York Times, Panettiere hired private security that same month to help keep Hickerson away. What did Panettiere say about their relationship? In 2022, Panettiere shared her thoughts on their relationship with People. “It was a very dark and complicated time in my life. But a lot of women go through what I went through, and I want people to know it’s okay to ask for help,” she said. Related Article Vale Overdose suspected in Hayden Panettiere death as emergency audio emerges “I am trying to live in a place of understanding. I think [Hickerson] has done his time and was willing to get help. I think about the things I have done in my life that people forgave me for. Making amends is a really important thing that you learn in treatment. And it gives you a lot of inner peace.”



In her memoir, Panettiere was open about her own struggles with alcohol addiction and substance abuse. In 2015, she checked herself into a treatment facility to get professional help for postpartum depression, and in early 2020, she entered an in-patient treatment centre for alcohol and opioid addiction. She also expressed how she felt while Hickerson was serving time in jail. “I needed him to admit his wrongs and change because of them, but I didn’t want to traumatise him in an irreversible way,” she wrote. His assets will be confiscated, and his companies were fined a combined 15.82 billion yuan ($3.3 billion). The move draws a curtain on what for years was one of China’s great success stories. Hui had binged on debt during Evergrande’s expansion, turning it into the world’s most indebted developer as he transformed the property giant into a sprawling conglomerate.



But Chinese authorities concluded that his rise was built on deception. They said Hui had perpetrated a massive financial fraud that included inflating assets and concealing liabilities. Related Article Opinion

Inside China China’s property cancer is spreading through its economy Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In 2017, Hui had a net worth of $US45.3 billion ($63.3 billiion), the highest in Asia, according to Forbes. By 2023, it had shrunk to an estimated $US3 billion. On Thursday, the court in Shenzhen ordered the confiscation of all his personal property. In April, Hui had pleaded guilty in a Chinese court to charges including illegally taking public deposits and fundraising fraud. “The amount involved in the crime is exceptionally large, the circumstances are particularly heinous, exceptionally heavy economic losses have been caused, and the harm to society is extremely grave,” a report from state media outlet Xinhua wrote, adding that Evergrande and Hui “must be severely punished in accordance with the law.”



Evergrande and Hui were also found guilty of fraudulently issuing securities, violating information disclosure rules as well as bribery. Meanwhile, the founder was accused of embezzling company assets through dividend mechanisms. The sentence doesn’t bring an end to the numerous legal fights surrounding Evergrande. The company is now in liquidation, with an army of creditors inside and outside of China poring over its assets in the hopes of recovering some of their heavy losses. During its prime, Evergrande built more than 1300 projects across 280 cities. Bloomberg Rags to riches Hui, also known as Xu Jiayin in Mandarin, was born in Henan province in 1958 and grew up in poverty. Encouraged by the prospect of Deng Xiaoping’s economic reform plan, the son of a wood cutter quit his job at a steel firm in 1992 and later began developing property in Guangzhou, the provincial capital of Guangdong. He then founded Evergrande in 1996 and rode the wave of China’s unprecedented real estate boom.



Evergrande, which means “permanence and greatness” in Chinese, relied on heavy borrowing to fuel its growth, becoming the largest dollar-debt borrower among its peers and for a time the country’s biggest developer by sales. During its prime, the firm built more than 1300 projects across 280 cities. Supercharged by real estate riches, it also expanded its reach into industries ranging from bottled water to professional soccer and electric vehicles. For a long time, Evergrande skirted liquidity scares by tapping tycoons in China and Hong Kong to buy the firm’s stock and bonds. Hui also turned to his own suppliers and retail investors for financial backing. But Beijing’s crackdown on the property sector since 2020 capped its borrowing capacity, effectively cutting Hui off from credit markets. Hui’s charges follow a long list of harsh actions by Chinese authorities against corporate magnates. The sentence doesn’t bring an end to the numerous legal fights surrounding Evergrande. The company is now in liquidation, with an army of creditors inside and outside of China poring over its assets in the hopes of recovering some of their heavy losses. Anbang Group’s former chairman, Wu Xiaohui, was sentenced to 18 years in prison for fraud and embezzlement in 2018. That same year, China Huarong Asset Management Co. Chairman Lai Xiaomin was arrested amid a corruption scandal before being executed in 2021 on charges including bribery. HNA Group chairman Chen Feng was detained a few months later along with chief executive officer Tan Xiangdong for unspecified crimes.



Evergrande defaulted on its debt in late 2021. Following failed restructuring attempts, it was given a winding up order in Hong Kong in 2024, marking a significant escalation in the unravelling of the sector. Later that year, a mainland Chinese court accepted a liquidation application filed against one of its major onshore units. Hui was taken away by Chinese police in 2023 and held under so-called residential surveillance — a type of police action that falls short of formal detention or arrest. Apart from a company filing confirming Hui being put under control, Chinese authorities had remained tight-lipped about his status since then. Related Article Opinion

Inside China The Chinese dream has turned into a nightmare In 2024, Chinese regulators accused Evergrande’s main onshore unit of inflating more than 560 billion yuan of revenue by recognising sales in advance, an alleged fraud that dwarfs that of Luckin Coffee and Enron. China then suspended the operations of PricewaterhouseCoopers, Evergrande’s long-time auditor, for six months and imposed fines. Much of Hui’s known wealth was derived from his controlling stake in Evergrande and the cash dividends he’s received from the company since its 2009 listing in Hong Kong. Hui had pocketed more than $US7 billion over the past decade, thanks to the firm’s generous payouts, according to Bloomberg calculations.
